R1062.rationale:
Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes.
The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After launching Operation Ghazab lil Haq on 21 February, Pakistani authorities declared open war against Afghanistan's Interim Taliban Authority. Despite a two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April negotiated by China, these attacks have continued, forming a pattern of ‘coercive diplomacy’ between the two countries. This coercive diplomacy has seen fighting continue until it becomes less productive for either side, at which point they briefly return to negotiations until a new security incident restarts the cycle. This pattern is expected to persist in waves over the next three to six months rather than resolve into a stable ceasefire.
The current tension heightens protection risks for civilians in border-adjacent Afghan provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika), including casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, as well as exposure to explosive remnants of war and unexploded ordnance in areas affected by shelling.
Displacement towards other regions of Afghanistan is expected to persist over the next three to six months. The closure of and restricted movement at the Torkham, Chaman, and other crossings along the Durand Line, whether from active conflict or checkpoint closures, could trap civilians in insecure areas or block access to services on the other side. Host communities already sheltering IDPs and returnees face added strain, raising the risk of tension and disputes over limited resources and services.
The closure of border crossings has also halted transit flows and delayed humanitarian and commercial supplies. Afghanistan is highly dependent on food imports, as domestic production cannot meet national demand. This dependence, combined with the depletion of harvest stocks in September and declining agricultural labour opportunities from the seasonal downturn in October, is likely to worsen food insecurity. As a result, market dependence is expected to increase, reducing household income and heightening the risk of food consumption gaps. ([CFR 18/03/2026](https://www.cfr.org/articles/why-are-the-afghan-taliban-and-pakistan-in-an-open-war), [The Guardian 29/06/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jun/29/pakistan-deadly-airstrikes-afghanistan-border), [HRW 15/07/2026](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/07/15/pakistani-strikes-in-afghanistan-raise-civilian-casualty-concerns), [UNAMA 11/05/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/English%20-%20UNAMA%20HRS%20paper%20on%20cross-border%20civilian%20casualties%20-%20Jan-Mar%202026_Updated_11.05.26.pdf), [WFP 26/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/food-security-under-pressure-impacts-middle-east-crisis-and-pakistan-conflict-afghanistan-june-2026), [OCHA 28/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-situation-update-4-humanitarian-impact-afghanistan-pakistan-military-escalation-28-april-2026), [NPR 03/04/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/03/g-s1-116299/pakistan-says-a-new-round-of-peace-talks-with-afghanistan-is-underway-in-china), [Reuters 02/04/2026](https://www.aol.com/articles/pakistan-says-talks-afghanistan-end-071917568.html), [UNAMA 29/06/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/en/news/unama-statement-on-civilian-casualties))

R1038.rationale:
In early April 2026, the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) attacked a Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) position in Tillabéri, marking the first reported direct confrontation between the two groups in Niger after years of rivalry concentrated in Mali and Burkina Faso. Tillabéri is already one of the most affected areas in the central Sahel, where violence against civilians, displacement, and weak state presence have created acute protection risks. Tillabéri recorded the highest level of civilian targeting across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger in 2025, with over 1,200 of Niger’s 1,939 civilian fatalities occurring there, primarily attributed to ISSP, followed by JNIM and the Nigerien military. 
The risk of escalation is linked to the geographic expansion of JNIM–ISSP competition into western Niger, where both groups are increasingly competing for territorial influence, recruitment networks, road axes, and local economies. Recent attacks on military installations in Tahoua city, including the Base Aérienne 401 and the 42nd battalion headquarters in March 2026, indicate that insecurity is increasingly affecting strategic urban and military locations beyond the main rural border areas of Tillabéri. These developments have already disrupted humanitarian operations, with UNHAS flights temporarily suspended because of insecurity and repercussions on humanitarian access. 
Over the next six months, escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger could mirror patterns seen in Mali and Burkina Faso, where rivalry expansion led to heightened violence against civilians, mass displacement, and further erosion of state control. Armed group competition and pressure on key road axes will likely expand attacks into previously less-affected communes and towns in western Niger, leading to a deterioration in civilian security and access to services. Both groups may intensify targeting of populations perceived to support rivals, particularly rural communities in contested border areas of Tillabéri, as well as displaced and host communities, leaving civilians vulnerable to crossfire, accusations of collaboration, and illegal taxation. Tillabéri’s existing high baseline of civilian harm, combined with weak state presence, protracted displacement, and fragile livelihoods, could amplify the impact of further escalation. New displacement, exacerbated food insecurity, and deepened humanitarian access constraints are likely as groups compete for recruitment and resources in this strategic border zone. ([Reuters 09/04/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/fighting-between-sahel-based-jihadist-rivals-spills-into-niger-2026-04-09/), [Crisis Group 20/02/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/rpt/africa/sahel-west-africa/321-le-jnim-et-le-dilemme-de-lexpansion-au-dela-du-sahel), [RFI 09/03/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260309-niger-des-groupes-terroristes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-pour-la-premi%C3%A8re-fois-l-importante-ville-de-tahoua))

R1069.rationale:
By 28 August 2026, an estimated 700–1,000 military personnel were conducting clearance operations around the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Yebyu township after a late-June order to protect the strategic projects. Since 9 July, fighting, raids, arson, looting, arbitrary arrests, and killings have displaced more than 4,500 people from eight Nabule villages. Renewed fighting near the SEZ from 21–22 August caused further civilian displacement. More than 2,000 people were displaced from ten villages in Thayetchaung township in August.
The concentration of military deployments around the project area, following orders to protect strategic infrastructure and agreements to revive the project, indicates that the operation is intended to secure the SEZ. The SEZ is a long-stalled port and industrial zone planned to include a deep-sea port, coal-fired power plant, oil refinery, and liquefied natural gas facilities. The risk is more immediate because Myanmar and Russia revived the project in 2025, signed a June 2026 power plant agreement, and included the Dawei port, refinery, and power plant in their August Moscow agreements. The timing of these deals and the deployment, alongside clashes with the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) near Wet Chaung, makes control of the project area a current strategic objective rather than a remote development scenario.
Over the next six months, military efforts to secure the SEZ are likely to include attempts to control Highway 8, the main north–south route through Tanintharyi, and the Dawei–Htee Khee road, which connects the project area through Myitta to the Thailand border. These routes are important for moving troops and supplies and would support future port and SEZ operations. Continued resistance activities by the KNLA, National Unity Government-affiliated People’s Defence Forces, and other local resistance groups operating in and around the Dawei SEZ could trigger further military sweeps, preventing safe returns and causing new and repeated displacement. Prolonged separation from homes, farms, and plantations will reduce food production and household income, increasing dependence on markets and host communities and worsening food, shelter, and health needs. ([Reuters 21/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/myanmar-military-offensive-targets-land-russia-backed-port-project-2026-08-21/), [HURFOM 25/08/2026](https://rehmonnya.org/renewed-fighting-in-dawei-sez-displaces-more-civilians-in-yebyu-township/), [ACLED 06/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/myanmar-outlook-fighting-set-intensify-center-country), [EU SEE 13/08/2026](https://eusee.hivos.org/alert/junta-troops-abduct-and-execute-lgbtq-youth-humanitarian-aid-workers-during-clearance-operation-for-russian-backed-dawei-sez/), [CRPH 08/06/2026](https://www.crphsupportgroup.no/post/moscow-agrees-to-build-power-plant-for-myanmar-s-stalled-dawei-sez), [DVB 26/08/2026](https://english.dvb.no/military-troop-surge-triggers-clashes-with-knla-near-stalled-dawei-sez-in-tanintharyi-region/), [HURFOM 16/07/2026](https://rehmonnya.org/junta-regiments-torch-houses-and-force-na-bu-lell-residents-to-flee/), [HURFOM 18/08/2026](https://rehmonnya.org/700-junta-soldiers-advance-into-tha-yet-chaung-forcing-thousands-of-villagers-to-flee/), [The Irrawaddy 22/07/2026](https://www.irrawaddy.com/news/burma/three-aid-workers-found-dead-as-myanmar-troops-clear-dawei-sez.html), [The Irrawaddy 28/08/2026](https://www.irrawaddy.com/news/burma/regime-attacks-surge-around-russia-backed-dawei-sez.html), [The Irrawaddy 02/11/2018](https://www.irrawaddy.com/news/myanmar-thailand-jointly-upgrade-highway-border-dawei-sez.html))

R1043.rationale:
Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border.

This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into contested spaces where violence increasingly follows smuggling and supply networks. Recent attacks suggest a shift from incidental spillover to deliberate projection of force into Chadian territory.

The conflict is also aggravating existing vulnerabilities in Chad. Fractures within cross-border Zaghawa community networks, which remain influential within Chad’s security apparatus, have deepened as communities react to violence in Darfur and perceptions of Chad’s involvement in the conflict. Continued violence in Darfur, combined with Chad’s historical role in Sudanese proxy conflicts, increases the risk of elite defections, armed realignments, and renewed cross-border mobilisation. Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may also re-emerge, including support to armed groups and militias operating across the border, increasing the likelihood of retaliatory attacks and further regional destabilisation.

Over the next one to three months, further RSF incursions, SAF-backed proxy activity, or competition over border corridors could increase cross-border violence, displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad. Additional attacks or retaliations would likely worsen conditions in provinces already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees, further straining regional services, humanitarian operations, and community relations. The risk is not limited to humanitarian spillover and increasingly involves the possibility of sustained confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces. ([Africa Center for Strategic Studies 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf), [ACLED 08/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/africa-overview-april-2026), [Global Initiative 06/03/2026](https://globalinitiative.net/analysis/how-border-criminal-economies-are-drawing-chad-further-into-sudans-conflict/), [ISS Africa 03/04/2025](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions), [RFI 13/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260513-tchad-de-nouvelles-frappes-enregistr%C3%A9es-%C3%A0-la-fronti%C3%A8re-soudanaise-font-craindre-le-pire), [UNHCR 18/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/core-emergency-situation-chad-update-arrivals-sudan-17-may-2026), [UNFPA 15/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unfpa-situation-report-chad-humanitarian-response-1-30-april-2026))

comments.text: I'd push back on "deliberate". From the Darfur side, most of these incidents look like fights over fuel and supply routes that spill across the line, not a plan to strike Chad. The risk is real, but for now I read it as spillover.

The direction looks right, but two months feels tight. I don't know Chad closely, but conflicts like this tend to move in bursts, and both sides still have more to gain inside Sudan. I'd rate this lower for January and higher for later in 2027.

I agreed at first, but the point about supply routes here changed my mind. Most of what I hear around Tine is about fuel and smuggling disputes, not fighters trying to hold ground inside Chad. Worrying, but not sustained confrontation yet.

Agree, and the economic side deserves more weight. When a conflict runs on fuel and gold routes, the fighting follows the money. If those corridors close, prices in the border towns will move long before the headlines do.

I've seen this pattern on other borders. Once armed groups depend on a crossing for supplies, it stops being a border incident and becomes a target. The infrastructure trigger is the one I'd watch: a strike on Amdjarass would change the whole picture.

Agree. Working in Niger, I've seen how quickly a border area changes once armed groups move freely, and how slowly humanitarian access comes back afterwards. I'd plan for access problems before casualties rise.

Attached a market bulletin that fits this reading. Supply routes are where armed groups earn and spend, so markets often show trouble early. I know this pattern from Colombia's border regions more than from Chad, so take it as a comparison.

Agree with the rating, but I'd add local deals to the picture. In Syria, crossings changed hands through negotiation as often as through fighting, and civilians were caught out either way. Could the same happen around Tine?

The rains are over, so the tracks around Adré are passable again. That helps aid trucks, but it helps armed groups too. Sites in Ouaddaï and Wadi Fira are already overcrowded, so new arrivals would have nowhere to go.

Attached a situation update. Families in West Darfur are deciding on rumours as much as on attacks, so one strike near Adré could move people in both directions at once. Refugees and returnees would need help on the same road.

R1059.rationale:
After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures.
This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025.
This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against communities, including curfews and checkpoints. Ahead of the anticipated offensive, NSAGs are expected to intensify operations to consolidate territorial control, while retaliatory actions during the crackdown could further increase civilian harm. In response, the elected President has proposed Plan Colombia 2.0, aimed at recovering NSAG-controlled territory, eradicating coca cultivation and illegal mining (the primary financing sources for armed groups), and securing record investment in state armed forces, with the political and financial support of the US Government.
As a result, July, the month preceding the new Government's inauguration, is expected to see an intensification of NSAG violence as armed groups seek to consolidate territorial control and prepare ahead of the anticipated military offensive. Over the first 90-day period (August–October), a marked increase in armed clashes with state forces is expected, a trend that should persist throughout the remainder of 2026. These dynamics will directly affect civilian populations in the departments highlighted, where most rural and Indigenous communities reside.
Planned government reforms, including major cuts to state bureaucracy and measures targeting officials linked to the previous administration, could also increase political tensions and trigger social mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the risk.
A historic ‘Super El Niño’ event, forecast to intensify through late 2026, is expected to compound these dynamics. Authorities are warning of extreme heat, drought, and water shortages, with national implications for food security. This adds further pressure on communities in the departments covered by this risk, where access to food is already constrained by confinement and mobility restrictions linked to armed group activity. 
([El País 21/06/2026](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/elecciones-presidenciales/2026-06-21/las-propuestas-de-abelardo-de-la-espriella-seguridad-de-mano-dura-reduccion-del-estado-y-libertades-tributarias.html), [FIP 30/01/2026](https://ideaspaz.org/publicaciones/investigaciones-analisis/2026-01/27-000-combatientes-y-record-en-disputas-el-deterioro-de-la-seguridad-marca-el-inicio-de-2026), [Valora Analitik 17/12/2025](https://www.valoraanalitik.com/grupos-armados-en-colombia-aumentaron-casi-70-desde-2022-crecen-homicidios-y-secuestros/), [Defensores de la Patria accessed 06/07/2026](https://defensoresdelapatria.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/PROPUESTAS-DEL-TIGRE.pdf), [AJ 22/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/22/far-right-de-la-espriella-elected-colombia-president-whats-next), [NPR 21/06/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/21/nx-s1-5865676/delaespriella-colombia-election), [Atlantic Council 22/06/2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/experts-react-what-a-president-abelardo-de-la-espriella-means-for-colombia-and-beyond/), [The City Paper 21/05/2026](https://thecitypaperbogota.com/news/colombia-on-guard-as-super-el-nino-threatens-record-heat-drought-and-food-security/))

R1066.rationale:
Violence involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) is rising after five years of declining lethality in the Lake Chad Basin. More than 300 clashes involving the two groups were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, 30% above the previous quarter, while militant Islamist-linked fatalities increased by 28% over the past year, reaching their highest level since 2015. Nigeria accounted for 87% of these fatalities, with Borno remaining the expected epicentre, followed by affected areas of Adamawa and Yobe.
The escalation is expected to be driven by two related developments. While regional forces have concentrated military operations against ISWAP, Boko Haram has regrouped and rebuilt its capacity to launch coordinated attacks against military bases. At the same time, the May killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal Al Minuki is expected to trigger retaliatory attacks and greater competition between factions for territorial influence and legitimacy. ISWAP has overrun at least 16 Nigerian military bases over the past year, while its increasing use of improvised explosive devices and reconnaissance drones enhances its capacity to identify, isolate, and attack military positions, increasing the operational threat posed by the group.
Over the next three to six months, there is a very high probability that intensified insurgent attacks and military counteroperations will increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints across the basin. Violence is expected to remain concentrated in Borno, with continued spillover into Adamawa and Yobe, where Boko Haram and ISWAP are likely to intensify attacks on civilians, military positions, and transport routes. Escalating violence in northeastern Nigeria is expected to generate additional refugee movements into Niger's Diffa region, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may contribute to increased attacks, abductions, and disruptions to fishing and trade in Cameroon’s Far North, as well as renewed displacement and protection risks in Chad’s Lac province. These cross-border displacement dynamics and parallel insecurity are expected to reverse recent stabilisation gains and generate additional humanitarian needs across the Lake Chad Basin. ([ICG 09/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/oth/chad-cuba-horn-africa-pakistan/horizon-july-december-2026), [OCHA 07/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/nigeria/lake-chad-basin-humanitarian-overview-2026-29-june-2026), [OCHA 29/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/nigeria/lake-chad-basin-humanitarian-overview-29-april-2026), [RFI 23/06/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260623-aux-confins-nord-du-cameroun-une-commune-enclav%C3%A9e-sous-une-pression-jihadiste-constante), [AJ 18/05/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/18/how-iswap-and-boko-haram-are-reshaping-the-lake-chad-basin), [UNHCR 02/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/cameroon/lake-chad-basin-regional-protection-and-displacement-crisis-humanitarian-priorities-and-funding-needs-across-cameroon-chad-niger-and-nigeria-june-december-2026), [UNHCR 03/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/cameroon/unhcr-warns-lake-chad-basin-tipping-point-violence-and-displacement-surge), [ACLED 19/05/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/violence-involving-boko-haram-and-islamic-state-west-africa-province-rising), [ACSS 06/04/2026](https://africacenter.org/spotlight/2026a-mig-widening-militant-islamist-threat/))

R1037.rationale:
The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.
Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again. ([ICG 25/03/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war), [ISS 30/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/race-against-time-to-stabilise-south-sudan-as-elections-loom), [OCHA 12/02/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-january-2026), [OCHA 16/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-update-1-17-april-2026), [MSF 30/01/2026](https://www.msf.org/south-sudan-government-blocks-opposition-held-areas-humanitarian-access))

triggers.title: Cancellation of the December 2026 elections
triggers.description: With the 2018 peace process now dead, the December 2026 elections represented one of the few remaining frameworks for legitimate political transition — yet the prerequisites for a credible vote do not exist. The National Elections Commission remains unfunded, forces have not been unified, and active fighting makes campaigning impossible across large parts of the country. A further cancellation would likely be interpreted by opposition groups as a permanent consolidation of power by Kiir's government, deepening ethnic grievances and accelerating recruitment into armed factions Sources: ([Crisis Group 26/03/2026 https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war]) Completion rate: 60% Completion rate history: 23-04-2026: 60% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes - 100% would be the election being formally cancelled leading to deepening conflict. triggers.title: Economic collapse drives predatory violence by armed actors on both sides
triggers.description: Prolonged economic decline has left both sides severely weakened. Depleted state coffers and irregular pay have driven desertions and eroded morale, leaving government forces overstretched and increasingly reliant on proxy militias. With formal resourcing exhausted, offensives by government forces and militias have become as much about extracting taxes and looting civilian populations as achieving military objectives. Opposition forces face comparable pressures, with communal militias motivated more by the prospect of loot than political strategy. As both sides are compelled to prey on the communities they operate in, this dynamic risks transforming localised clashes into a self-sustaining cycle of violence, in which continued conflict becomes an economic necessity for armed actors, reducing incentives to negotiate and compounding an already acute humanitarian crisis. Sources: ([Crisis Group 26/03/2026 https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war]) Completion rate: 30% Completion rate history: 23-04-2026: 30% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 23-04-2026 Last update: 23-04-2026

triggers.title: Entanglement with the war in Sudan
triggers.description: South Sudan's conflict risks becoming entangled with the war in Sudan. Though Juba has maintained official neutrality, its close links to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which control much of Sudan's border with South Sudan, are widely observed. The Sudanese army is suspected of reactivating ties with Nuer opposition forces in a bid to pressure Kiir and disrupt RSF supply lines — a dynamic that, if confirmed, would effectively transform Upper Nile into a proxy theatre of Sudan's war. Compounding this, Uganda's continued military backing of Kiir is not guaranteed; Kampala's willingness to underwrite his survival is uncertain given South Sudan's economic collapse and Uganda's competing regional commitments. A withdrawal of Ugandan support, combined with increasing Sudanese entanglement, could significantly alter the military balance, accelerating conflict escalation and further collapsing humanitarian access Sources: ([Crisis Group 24/03/2026] https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war) Completion rate: 20% Completion rate history: 23-04-2026: 20% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 23-04-2026 Last update: 23-04-2026

R1048.rationale:
The RSF offensive launched in early 2026 against Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) positions in Baw county opened a new front in Blue Nile state. This has significantly increased the likelihood of conflict spreading to previously unaffected areas to the north, particularly Ed Damazine, the state capital, as well as the strategic corridor leading to the Roseires Dam. By advancing in Blue Nile state, RSF seeks to strengthen its position to recapture and control central Sudan, later opening a route through Sennar state. 
Following heavy territorial losses in 2025, including entire states in central Sudan, RSF has reconstituted its operational capacity through its alliance with Abdelaziz Adam al Hilu's Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N/Al Hilu). Access to terrain under its control has provided RSF with defensive depth, cross-border supply lines, and logistical continuity. This enables it to sustain multifront operations and power its advance in Blue Nile, positioning the RSF for a prolonged and expanded offensive rather than a short-term tactical push and increasing the likelihood of escalation beyond the current front lines.
External facilitation further compounds these dynamics. SAF has repeatedly accused South Sudan and Ethiopia of enabling this mobilisation, with satellite imagery from February 2026 showing a logistics camp near the Ethiopian border in Benishangul Gumz despite official Ethiopian denial. R1061.rationale:
There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.
Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. With far-right coalition partners Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism continuing to advocate expanding Israeli control over Gaza and negotiations on a durable ceasefire and post-conflict governance remaining stalled, the Likud-led caretaker government, in place since the Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, will very probably prioritise maintaining operational momentum in Gaza while avoiding the political and military risks associated with a large-scale offensive.

Territorial expansion is expected to continue through a combination of military and engineering measures that progressively transform temporary military positions into more permanent areas of control. Israeli forces are likely to continue advancing the Yellow Line through localised incursions supported by repeated evacuation orders, the demolition of buildings and agricultural land, and the construction of additional military infrastructure, including outposts, surveillance positions, access roads, trenches, and earthen barriers. Recent satellite imagery indicates that Israel has already constructed more than 23km of earth berms and trenches along parts of the Yellow Line, creating a fortified corridor that extends across central Gaza and, in some locations, beyond the original ceasefire demarcation. These measures are likely to be accompanied by the continued expansion of military exclusion zones and restrictions on civilian movement, allowing Israeli forces to consolidate control without undertaking a single large-scale offensive. ([BIPP 06/03/2026](https://www.bakerinstitute.org/research/israeli-elections-cast-doubt-gaza-peace-plan), [NPR 23/07/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/07/23/nx-s1-5891506/israel-will-hold-elections-this-fall-gadi-eisenkott-could-be-the-next-prime-minister), [Chatham House 22/07/2026](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/07/israels-general-election-will-be-no-other), [CNN 20/07/2026](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/07/20/middleeast/israel-far-right-settlements-gaza-intl), [The Conversation 24/07/2026](https://theconversation.com/as-israel-prepares-for-october-election-the-government-is-accelerating-its-land-grab-in-the-west-bank-and-gaza-288286), [DAWN 21/07/2026](https://dawnmena.org/israels-elections-will-not-end-its-genocidal-and-expansionist-policies/), [ACLED accessed 25/07/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [Haaretz 07/07/2026](https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/israel-security/2026-07-07/ty-article/.premium/as-netanyahu-battles-for-votes-he-could-reignite-gaza-fighting/0000019f-390c-d62f-a39f-7d2c08a00000), [LWJ 19/10/2025](https://www.longwarjournal.org/archives/2025/10/profiles-of-anti-hamas-militias-in-the-gaza-strip.php), [AP accessed 01/08/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-gaza-yellow-line-barrier-ceasefire-941ed80f6d4398ce88916f6b08753dd8), [TOI 17/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-votes-on-official-dispersal-of-parliament-wrapping-up-final-legislative-blitz/), [AJ 22/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/22/creeping-death-israel-weaponises-yellow-line-to-annex-gaza))

R1067.rationale:
Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities.
Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting.
ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. This indicates Badakhshan province is becoming a potential point for national conflict risk.
The province has valuable mineral deposits, including gold and lapis lazuli, and has long been contested. Recent clashes were triggered by the ITA suspension of gold mining activities in parts of the province to disarm fighters of opposition groups.
Clashes have occurred across multiple districts in 2026, including a brief seizure of the Yaftal-e Sufla district headquarters and Afghanistan Freedom Front clashes with ITA forces in Zebak in July. Repeated fighting over district centres risks triggering intermittent displacement as families flee active front lines and may expose residents to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and casualties. Badakhshan’s current context indicates a risk of rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating food security outlook. ([ACLED 20/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/taliban-losing-control-northern-afghanistan), [Hasht-e Subh 26/08/2026](https://8am.media/eng/badakhshan-health-centers-mothers-children/), [Amu TV 20/05/2026](https://amu.tv/240020/#google_vignette), [ACLED 13/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/five-years-seizing-power-afghanistan-internal-tensions-test-talibans-vulnerabilities), [Afghanistan International 17/08/2026](https://www.afintl.com/en/202608171939), [ACLED accessed 27/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/platform/trends), [FEWS NET 25/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-el-nino-conditions-expected-be-key-driver-202627-agricultural-season-june-25-2026), [TCA 25/08/2026](https://timesca.com/badakhshan-fighting-raises-risks-for-tajikistan-and-uzbekistan/), [SWJ 07/08/2026](https://smallwarsjournal.com/2026/08/07/badakhshan-and-the-first-signs-of-a-localized-anti-taliban-insurgency-in-afghanistan/))

R1072.rationale:
Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) activity in northern Mozambique has increasingly shifted towards mobile, small-group operations as a response to intensified military pressure from Mozambican security forces and their regional partners. Increased patrols, aerial surveillance, and continued counterinsurgency operations have reduced non-state armed groups' capacity to hold territory. As a result, ISM have increasingly dispersed from areas under intensified military pressure in Macomia district towards southern and western Cabo Delgado province. ISM have moved through Quissanga, Mecufi, and Meluco towards Ancuabe and Chiure districts, while other groups moved west towards Montepuez district and subsequently towards Niassa province. One group also crossed into Erati district in Nampula province.
Over the next six months, continued military pressure in Cabo Delgado is expected to further disperse ISM fighters towards areas with weaker security coverage. Remote forested areas and limited state presence in parts of Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, which have had some pockets of attacks, provide opportunities for small groups to move and conduct more attacks. ISM have increasingly targeted informal gold mining sites for looting and ransom, while attacks on vehicles and road users have generated additional income through extortion. In Niassa, the July–November hunting season also increases the presence of hunting camps, tourism operators, and vehicles in remote areas, creating potential high-value targets for ransom and material gains. If ISM establish a presence in Montepuez, Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, these activities could provide alternative sources of revenue and sustain their operations. ([ACLED 05/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-august-2026), [IOM 24/06/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/mozambique-movement-alert-report-163-24-june-2026), [ACLED 08/09/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-september-2026), [OCHA 08/09/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/mozambique/mozambique-2026-humanitarian-response-conflict-overview-july-2026-enpt), [Gov.UK accessed 22/09/2026](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/mozambique/regional-risks))

R1052.rationale: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) face growing pressure from key external allies, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the US, to distance itself from allied armed groups with political Islam leanings, including the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. This creates a risk of fragmentation within SAF's alliance structure, as attempts to contain, integrate, or undermine these groups could provoke resistance. SAF remains operationally dependent on allied armed groups for manpower, mobilisation, funding channels, and battlefield capacity across multiple fronts, making coercive integration difficult. Tensions have also emerged between SAF and factions linked to JEM, the Joint Forces, and other groups present in civilian and commercial areas in Khartoum. US designation and sanctions linked to the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood and Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade add further external pressure on SAF to disengage from these groups. If SAF pursues integration or restrictions while these actors retain military leverage and local positions, tensions could escalate into localised clashes, checkpoint competition, and fragmented territorial control in Khartoum and central Sudan. ([Atlantic Council 26/01/2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/sudan-muslim-brotherhood-iran-us-terror/), [CT 12/03/2026](https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/africa-file-march-12-2026-islamist-militias-sudan), [The Interpreter 26/11/2025](https://www.lowyinstitute.org/the-interpreter/armed-groups-sudan-conflict), [US DOS 09/03/2026](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/03/sudanese-muslim-brotherhood), [USDT 12/09/2025](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0253), [ST 07/03/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/311465))

R1065.rationale:
On 13 July 2026, the Iran-backed de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) announced the end of a de facto period of de-escalation with Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen, increasing the risk of renewed cross-border and intra-Yemeni hostilities following a series of retaliatory actions. On the same day, the IRG said it had struck Sana'a International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, while the DFA accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the attack. The DFA subsequently retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks against Abha International Airport, marking the first attack on Saudi territory since the 2022 truce. On 20 July, the DFA announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, describing it as a response to Saudi restrictions on DFA-controlled airports and seaports. The DFA has already targeted several vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, in an attempt to enforce the blockade.
Fighting has also intensified between the DFA and the IRG along front lines in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta’iz, predating but compounded by the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations. Saudi Arabia is the main IRG backer, and the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations has already prompted expanded military involvement. From 24–25 July, the Saudi-led coalition conducted strikes in Al Hodeidah, while the IRG air force struck DFA missile and drone launch sites and weapons facilities in Ma'rib and Al Jawf. These developments indicate that the escalation has expanded beyond isolated cross-border retaliation, increasing the risk of sustained intra-Yemeni conflict.
The first cross-border attack on Saudi Arabia since the truce is significant because it signals that both parties are becoming increasingly willing to use direct military force to pursue their objectives, weakening one of the key restraints that has sustained the de facto ceasefire. Both Saudi Arabia and the DFA have incentives to avoid a renewed large-scale conflict. Saudi Arabia seeks to protect its economic interests and avoid another costly war, while the DFA is unlikely to escalate unless it perceives increased Saudi military involvement or an opportunity to improve its strategic position. A miscalculation could trigger the renewal of conflict. Further attacks on Saudi territory or attempts to enforce a blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait would increase the likelihood of expanded or sustained Saudi and international military involvement in the Red Sea and Yemen. Saudi Arabia has already announced plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition on 30 July 2026.
Escalations between the DFA and Saudi Arabia would likely intensify fighting between the DFA and the Saudi-backed IRG, further restricting humanitarian access. Saudi air strikes on seaports and airports would disrupt commercial and humanitarian imports, triggering new displacement. Supply chain disruptions would increase commodity prices and erode purchasing power. Any disruption to shipping through the Bab Al Mandab Strait would also have cascading impacts on regional and global supply chains while aggravating needs in a country where over 22 million people require humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure. ([OCHA 29/03/2026](https://yemen.un.org/en/312711-ocha-yemen-yemen-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-march-2026), [JP 25/07/2026](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-903606), [Reuters 24/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/yemen-teeters-towards-renewed-war-shadow-iran-conflict-2026-07-24/), [ICG 17/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/qna/middle-east-north-africa/yemen-iran-saudi-arabia/yemens-de-facto-truce-risk-how-prevent-return-war), [AJ 05/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/5/at-least-15-yemeni-government-troops-killed-in-hodeidah-fighting), [The Guardian 23/07/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/23/houthis-claim-attack-ship-tanker-saudi-arabia-red-sea), [Reuters 23/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/houthis-say-they-attacked-saudi-tankers-red-sea-threatening-new-chokepoint-iran-2026-07-23/), [Arab News 25/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2652234/middle-east), [SPA 25/07/2026](https://www.spa.gov.sa/en/N2640956))

R1068.rationale:
Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida.
Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israel a justification to intervene on behalf of the Druze and expand in southern Syria. The proposed corridor would connect the governorate with the Golan area, including Hader near Mount Hermon and Druze villages along the Syrian Golan. Although the proposal was previously rejected by the Syrian transitional Government, renewed violence or deterioration in As Sweida could bring it back into discussions and provide a pretext for expanding Israeli control or establishing protected access through southern Syria. While Israel framed its military intervention during the July 2025 violence as protecting the Druze, Druze opinion remains divided. One senior spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, has welcomed Israeli involvement, while the other two have consistently rejected foreign interference, and As Sweida's Druze security chief warned it had complicated reconciliation.
A second pathway is the activity of Israeli settlers seeking to establish a permanent presence. The Pioneers of Bashan,  an Israeli settler movement, have repeatedly attempted to cross into southern Syria and establish outposts, including around Hader and Mount Hermon, with their stated ambitions extending across As Sweida, Dar'a, and Quneitra governorates. More than 40 settlers entered the outskirts of Hader in April, while approximately 70–100 attempted to cross through Mount Hermon in July, followed by further attempts in August. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data indicates an upward trend in incursion attempts since April 2026, peaking sharply in July with six recorded events. Although the Israel Defense Forces have so far prevented permanent settlement, repeated attempts could increase pressure on Israeli authorities to eventually formalise such activity.
If either pathway materialises, further Israeli control and presence in southern Syria are likely to restrict civilian movement and access to agricultural land through additional checkpoints, patrols, and military restrictions. An expanded Israeli presence could also prompt resistance from Syrian government forces, as well as communities or armed groups in Quneitra and western Dar'a, increasing the probability of clashes around Israeli positions. ([Ynet 20/08/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/bktp9qfyxx), [Ynet 16/09/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/hyhslcujxx), [Jewish Policy Center 01/10/2025](https://www.jewishpolicycenter.org/2025/10/01/focus-on-the-druze/), [AA 31/07/2025](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/israeli-finance-minister-calls-for-humanitarian-corridor-to-syria-s-suwayda-for-druze-community/3646880), [Reuters 26/09/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-syria-talks-hit-snag-over-humanitarian-corridor-sources-say-2025-09-26/), [AP 29/07/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-syria-netanyahu-jewish-settlers-bashan-461c4c4f686d5cf74f0617a7e70ffa29), [TOI 29/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/fringe-settler-group-sneaking-into-syria-in-bid-to-claim-land-for-jewish-outpost/), [TOI 11/08/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/three-settlement-activists-illegally-enter-syria-overnight-are-detained-by-idf/), [L'Orient Today 14/07/2026](https://today.lorientlejour.com/article/1541299/who-are-the-bashan-pioneers-the-israeli-settlers-eyeing-southern-syria.html), [Arab News 06/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2649854/amp), [SOHR 27/06/2026](https://www.syriahr.com/en/383771/), [Enab Baladi 25/08/2026](https://english.enabbaladi.net/archives/2026/08/jordan-talks-fail-to-halt-israeli-incursions-in-southern-syria/), [EUAA accessed 28/07/2026](https://dip-aws.euaa.europa.eu/syria-security-situation/2142-territorial-control-and-main-armed-actors), [ACLED accessed 30/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [FP 24/07/2025](https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/07/24/risks-israel-druze-policy-syria/))

my_answers.text: Agree. Sieges of this size rarely stay local: once the main roads into a city are cut, the pressure moves to the next town that still has a market. I'd expect people to leave in stages, which makes the numbers easy to underestimate early on.

Agree on the direction. I know infrastructure risk better than Sudan itself, but when a supply corridor comes into drone range, hauliers and insurers change their behaviour before anything is hit. Deliveries slow first, and the damage shows up later in prices.

I'd rate this lower. Armies often close ranks after a mutiny when the threat outside is this visible, and I don't see a clear split yet. It would change my mind if units in the border regions started refusing orders.
Egypt will feel this through food and fertiliser prices and the currency, even if Red Sea shipping holds up.

triggers.title: Further escalation of the war in Gaza

rationale: The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.

Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again.

text: The risk has intensified after President Kiir dissolved the transitional government on 22 September, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December. The decree removed all five Vice Presidents, including the suspended First Vice President Riek Machar, dissolved the national and state legislatures, and replaced ministers and governors with caretaker appointees, ending the power-sharing arrangement set up under the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of Conflict in South Sudan. It followed amendments to the National Elections Act, signed on 21 September, that allow Kiir to remain in office with full powers throughout the election period. Kiir had also dismissed the chair of the National Elections Commission on 15 September without giving a reason. The South Sudan Opposition Movements Alliance has rejected the caretaker administration as illegitimate and the elections as a sham, and warned on 28 September that the crisis could lead to further violence and insecurity across the country. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, which had already warned in August that elections without safeguards and inclusive dialogue could fuel renewed conflict and atrocity crimes, said the window to prevent a return to 2013–2018 levels of violence and displacement is closing. Government and Sudan People's Liberation Army-in-Opposition forces continue to fight in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, a conflict that predates the election, and no escalation directly linked to the election has been reported so far. Any such escalation during the election period would add to displacement in areas where humanitarian access is already constrained.

vulnerability: South Sudan has experienced near-continuous conflict since independence in 2011, with the 2013–2018 civil war displacing nearly half the population and severely weakening governance structures. With the 2018 peace agreement now defunct, there is no functioning framework to contain further escalation. The economy has been in near-total collapse, with the GDP declining for five consecutive years, annual inflation reaching 183%, and the currency depreciating by 189% year-on-year in June 2025. By February 2025, nearly two million people were internally displaced, with an additional 300,000 displaced since the current crisis began. The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan estimates ten million people require humanitarian assistance, while funding has dropped to its lowest level since 2011, compounded by US aid cuts. Famine has already been recorded in Luakpiny/Nasir and Fangak, with 2.3 million people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) and 5.2 million in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) conditions. Aid weaponisation by both parties is an established pattern, with 28 health facilities in Jonglei alone looted or destroyed.
expected_impact: A return to full-scale civil war would rapidly overwhelm an already critically degraded humanitarian system. New displacement on the scale of the 2013–2018 civil war – when nearly half the population was uprooted – would exhaust regional absorption capacity, with Sudan at war and Ethiopia far from stable. As during the last civil war, secondary displacement flows towards North Africa and across the Mediterranean are likely. Famine risk, currently confined to Luakpiny/Nasir and Fangak, would spread rapidly as access collapses across conflict-affected areas. The established pattern of aid weaponisation would intensify; already, flight restrictions have suspended humanitarian flights to Akobo, Lankien, and Pieri, the bombing of the Médecins Sans Frontières Lankien hospital in February 2026 has left approximately 400,000 people without healthcare access, and aid workers have been forcibly evacuated from parts of Upper Nile state with 72 hours' notice – with government denial of access to opposition-held areas and systematic looting leaving the most vulnerable populations entirely unreachable. The already-underfunded humanitarian response would face collapse as needs outpace donor capacity, and the limited remaining health infrastructure – already severely degraded by looting and air strikes – would cease to function in the worst-affected areas.

rationale: In early April 2026, the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) attacked a Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) position in Tillabéri, marking the first reported direct confrontation between the two groups in Niger after years of rivalry concentrated in Mali and Burkina Faso. Tillabéri is already one of the most affected areas in the central Sahel, where violence against civilians, displacement, and weak state presence have created acute protection risks. Tillabéri recorded the highest level of civilian targeting across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger in 2025, with over 1,200 of Niger’s 1,939 civilian fatalities occurring there, primarily attributed to ISSP, followed by JNIM and the Nigerien military.

The risk of escalation is linked to the geographic expansion of JNIM–ISSP competition into western Niger, where both groups are increasingly competing for territorial influence, recruitment networks, road axes, and local economies. Recent attacks on military installations in Tahoua city, including the Base Aérienne 401 and the 42nd battalion headquarters in March 2026, indicate that insecurity is increasingly affecting strategic urban and military locations beyond the main rural border areas of Tillabéri. These developments have already disrupted humanitarian operations, with UNHAS flights temporarily suspended because of insecurity and repercussions on humanitarian access.

Over the next six months, escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger could mirror patterns seen in Mali and Burkina Faso, where rivalry expansion led to heightened violence against civilians, mass displacement, and further erosion of state control. Armed group competition and pressure on key road axes will likely expand attacks into previously less-affected communes and towns in western Niger, leading to a deterioration in civilian security and access to services. Both groups may intensify targeting of populations perceived to support rivals, particularly rural communities in contested border areas of Tillabéri, as well as displaced and host communities, leaving civilians vulnerable to crossfire, accusations of collaboration, and illegal taxation. Tillabéri’s existing high baseline of civilian harm, combined with weak state presence, protracted displacement, and fragile livelihoods, could amplify the impact of further escalation. New displacement, exacerbated food insecurity, and deepened humanitarian access constraints are likely as groups compete for recruitment and resources in this strategic border zone.

text: The risk increased during September as armed groups are expanding and consolidating overlapping areas of operation. Armed group activity continued to place pressure on Nigerien forces in western Niger during the second half of September, although no significant direct clashes between the Support Group for Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) were reported. On 26 September, two attacks attributed to Islamic State militants targeted Nigerien security forces near Abala in Tillabéri region and at Dabagu in Konni department, Tahoua region, killing 50–57 soldiers and gendarmes. The simultaneous attacks across two regions indicate ISSP's continued capacity to conduct high-impact operations against state forces beyond its core areas in Tillabéri. Violence also continued in Dosso region, with attacks reported in Dioundiou department during the second half of September, reinforcing indications of the southward expansion of armed group activity. While these developments increase pressure on security forces and confirm the continued geographic expansion of armed groups, there is not yet clear evidence of an escalation in direct JNIM–ISSP confrontation in Niger.

vulnerability: Populations in western Niger, particularly in Tillabéri and Tahoua regions, face high vulnerability because of protracted insecurity, displacement, and limited access to basic services. State presence remains weak in many rural areas, with armed groups exerting influence over local populations. Livelihoods are fragile and heavily affected by insecurity and restricted mobility, while access to healthcare, education, and markets is already constrained. Coping capacities are limited, as repeated shocks have eroded household resilience and reduced community-level support mechanisms.
expected_impact: An escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger would likely increase civilian casualties, displacement, and protection risks in areas already facing severe humanitarian needs. Tillabéri experienced a significant deterioration in security in the first quarter of 2026, with over 92,900 forcibly displaced people recorded in key departments and acute protection risks including killings, abductions, gender-based violence, and child protection concerns. Tahoua is also highly vulnerable, hosting 80,475 refugees, 65,892 IDPs, 10,597 returnees, and 52,805 asylum-seekers awaiting registration.

Further inter-group rivalry could expose communities in contested areas to reprisals for perceived collaboration with rival groups or state forces, while illegal taxation, extortion, and movement restrictions may further erode livelihoods and household coping capacities. Increased insecurity may also heighten risks of child recruitment, forced marriage, and other negative coping mechanisms, particularly among displaced and conflict-affected communities.

Humanitarian access constraints are also likely to worsen. In Tahoua, 582,061 people were estimated to be in need in 2025, with 40–50% located in hard-to-access areas. The imposition of armed escorts has already reduced operational capacity, with only one in five humanitarian missions carried out, while escort costs and administrative restrictions continue to limit the frequency of interventions.

Service disruption could aggravate already severe humanitarian conditions. Nationally, 3.9 million people, including 2.6 million children, require urgent humanitarian assistance, while 2.4 million people are projected to face severe food insecurity. Niger’s health and education systems are already under pressure, with 1.8 million people in need of health assistance and 1,097 schools non-functional, affecting 93,676 children. A further deterioration in Tillabéri and Tahoua would likely deepen protection needs, disrupt markets and basic services, and leave more conflict-affected communities under-assisted.

R1042.title: Continued coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades increase protection risks, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in Mali

triggers.title: Expansion of coordinated JNIM–FLA operations
triggers.description: Coordinated attacks by JNIM and the FLA against military bases, urban centres, and strategic infrastructure may continue or expand into additional regions, increasing territorial contestation and exposing civilians to heightened insecurity. Although likely tactical and temporary, continued operational coordination between both actors could allow simultaneous attacks across multiple regions and increase pressure on Malian forces. Sustained cooperation may also increase pressure on transport corridors and urban areas, particularly around central and northern Mali, while complicating military operations and humanitarian access. Further attacks on strategic towns or military positions could increase insecurity in areas previously considered comparatively more stable. Sources: ([RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260507-mali-combats-en-vue-dans-la-r%C3%A9gion-de-kidal-durcissement-du-blocus-jihadiste-sur-bamako\), [ACLED 30/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/heni-nsaibia-fall-kidal-turning-point-malis-conflic\)) Completion rate: 50% Completion rate history: 02-06-2026: 50% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if coordinated JNIM–FLA operations expand beyond current areas of activity and result in sustained attacks against additional strategic urban centres, transport corridors, or military installations across northern and central Mali. Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 02-06-2026 Last update: 08-06-2026

triggers.title: Intensification of military operations and retaliatory violence
triggers.description: In response to the coordinated attacks, Malian forces and allied armed actors may increase military operations, aerial strikes, and security measures in contested areas. Expanded military deployments around strategic towns, transport corridors, and urban centres may increase movement restrictions and insecurity for civilians. Escalating confrontations and the militarisation of strategic urban centres and transport routes may increase protection risks for civilians, including displacement, restrictions on movement, and disruptions to humanitarian operations and access to essential services. Communities perceived as supporting rival armed actors may also face heightened risks of reprisals, arbitrary restrictions, or violence by conflict parties. Sources: ([OCHA 08/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-bulletin-humanitaire-fevrier-mars-2026\), [Protection Cluster 03/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/note-de-protection-2eme-semestre-2025\)) Completion rate: 40% Completion rate history: 02-06-2026: 40% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if expanded military operations and retaliatory violence result in sustained movement restrictions, significant civilian displacement, widespread protection incidents, or major disruptions to humanitarian access and essential services in conflict-affected areas. Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 02-06-2026 Last update: 08-06-2026

rationale: Since late April 2026, the unprecedented operational coordination between Jama’at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA) has significantly increased pressure on Mali’s security apparatus and exposed vulnerabilities in state control across northern, central, and western regions. Over the next one to three months, three converging escalation dynamics will likely worsen humanitarian conditions significantly across Mali. The assassination of Defence Minister Gen. Sadio Camara on 25 April 2026 created a command vacuum in Mali's security apparatus leadership. As the junta’s chief military strategist and the primary architect of the partnership with Russia’s Africa Corps, his death is likely to severely hamper coordination of counter-offensive operations, make Malian-Russian tactical responses less cohesive, and embolden further advances by armed groups at a critical juncture of territorial contestation.

JNIM and the FLA are both targeting urban supply chains, favouring economic attrition strategies over military objectives. With the FLA explicitly signalling southward expansion following the capture of Kidal region, citing Gao and Tombouctou as its next targets, and JNIM threatening a full blockade of Bamako region along the Senegalese and Ivorian corridors, populations in major urban centres face mounting risks of acute fuel and food shortages. Critically low stocks in the capital mean any sustained suspension of truck traffic could rapidly disrupt electricity, healthcare, and water access for millions already living under severe humanitarian stress. Towns such as Bandiagara and Douentza are already becoming more isolated because of road insecurity and flight suspensions, significantly constraining humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people.

Escalating resource scarcity and growing disillusionment within the military following the Kidal withdrawal increase the likelihood of intra-junta fracture or countercoup in the coming weeks. Political instability at the centre would further constrain the junta's capacity to manage insurgent pressure, negotiate humanitarian access, and sustain basic service delivery, deepening civilian vulnerability across northern, central, and western Mali.

text: The risk continued to increase during the second half of September as JNIM sustained high-intensity operations in central Mali, further challenging state control and security along strategic corridors. Following its 10 September attack on the Dioura military camp, which killed more than 100 soldiers and resulted in more than 100 being captured, JNIM shelled the Sévaré air base for six consecutive nights between 14–19 September and attacked a forward operating base in Konna on 20 September. The attacks indicate JNIM's continued capacity to target major military positions and transport corridors in Mopti region, while supply routes to Bamako remain exposed to disruption by armed groups. Although no significant new joint operation by JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front was identified after the previous update, the sustained pressure by JNIM, alongside the continued presence and coordination capacity of both groups in northern Mali, maintains the risk of further territorial and humanitarian deterioration. Continued insecurity is likely to constrain population movement, trade, and humanitarian access, particularly across central and northern Mali.

vulnerability: Mali already faced severe humanitarian vulnerabilities before the April 2026 escalation. Persistent insecurity, repeated displacement, and limited state presence in northern and central regions have weakened access to healthcare, food, education, water, and protection services. According to OCHA, more than six million people were estimated to need humanitarian assistance in 2026, while insecurity and access constraints continue to limit humanitarian operations in several regions, particularly Gao, Kidal, Ménaka, Mopti, and parts of Tombouctou. Food insecurity and acute malnutrition remain elevated, especially in conflict-affected areas where population movement, market disruption, and loss of livelihoods reduce households’ coping capacities.

Since 2025, repeated attacks on transport corridors and fuel supply chains have increased the fragility of essential services and urban supply systems, including transportation and electricity production. Communities in blockaded or inaccessible areas have increasingly relied on potentially harmful coping strategies, including reducing food consumption, selling productive assets, and restricting movement. Humanitarian organisations continue to operate in Mali, but insecurity, bureaucratic constraints, and logistical disruptions limit response capacity and access to affected populations. The recent expansion of coordinated attacks towards strategic urban centres and transport routes will likely add further strain on already limited coping capacities and humanitarian response systems.
expected_impact: Continued conflict escalation is expected to significantly worsen humanitarian conditions across Mali over the next one to three months, compounding pre-existing vulnerabilities among an estimated 5.1 million people already needing assistance. Mali already hosts more than 414,000 IDPs, and the number is likely to surge as fighting intensifies in Gao and Tombouctou regions and spreads southward into Sikasso and Kayes regions. The conflict also threatens displacement of farming communities during the critical harvest season, which would amplify nationwide food insecurity risks. Mali's capacity to host refugees – including over 165,000 from Burkina Faso and Niger – will be further strained, placing additional pressure on already overstretched basic services in affected areas.

Attacks on transport corridors and supply routes may further disrupt fuel imports, commercial traffic, and market functionality, contributing to higher transportation and food prices and affecting the availability of essential goods and services. Continued insecurity along the Bamako–Kayes, Bamako–Ségou, and Bamako–Sikasso corridors could further affect the movement of fuel, food, and commercial goods into major urban centres. Additional pressure on electricity production and fuel supply systems could worsen existing disruptions to healthcare, water access, and telecommunications. Fuel shortages are already affecting ambulance referrals, emergency obstetric care, medical supply chains, and fuel-dependent health services in conflict-affected areas, particularly in northern and central Mali. If supply disruptions persist, urban populations in Bamako and secondary cities may experience prolonged electricity cuts, rising living costs, and reduced access to basic services.

Humanitarian responders are already facing significant operational constraints. Humanitarian flights have been repeatedly suspended, and WFP temporarily halted activities following the April attacks. Insecurity has made several destinations, including Ansongo, Douentza, Kidal, Niafunké, and Ménaka, partially or fully inaccessible. If attacks, blockades, and insecurity along key corridors persist, humanitarian access is likely to deteriorate further, delaying the delivery of assistance and reducing the reach of life-saving services.

Should political instability escalate into intra-junta fracture or a counter-coup, the collapse of security command structures would likely suspend humanitarian flights and road convoys entirely, cutting life-saving assistance to already inaccessible populations across northern and central Mali.

R1043.title: Escalating cross-border insecurity linked to the Sudan conflict increases protection risks and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad
