triggers.title: Renewed proxy mobilisation and cross-border armed group activity
triggers.description: Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may re-emerge through the mobilisation, arming, or support of rebel groups and allied militias operating along the border. Increased involvement of SAF-aligned groups, RSF-linked actors, Darfuri armed factions, or Chadian rebel networks could expand the conflict beyond isolated border incidents and increase the likelihood of retaliatory attacks on Chadian territory. Sources: ([ISS Africa 31/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions\), [Africa Center 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf\), [Global Initiative 06/03/2026](https://globalinitiative.net/analysis/how-border-criminal-economies-are-drawing-chad-further-into-sudans-conflict/\)) Completion rate: 20% Completion rate history: 02-06-2026: 20% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if armed groups, militias, or proxy actors operating across the Chad–Sudan border become actively involved in cross-border hostilities, resulting in sustained violence, retaliatory attacks, or territorial insecurity in eastern Chad. Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 02-06-2026 Last update: 08-06-2026

rationale: Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border.

This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into contested spaces where violence increasingly follows smuggling and supply networks. Recent attacks suggest a shift from incidental spillover to deliberate projection of force into Chadian territory.

The conflict is also aggravating existing vulnerabilities in Chad. Fractures within cross-border Zaghawa community networks, which remain influential within Chad’s security apparatus, have deepened as communities react to violence in Darfur and perceptions of Chad’s involvement in the conflict. Continued violence in Darfur, combined with Chad’s historical role in Sudanese proxy conflicts, increases the risk of elite defections, armed realignments, and renewed cross-border mobilisation. Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may also re-emerge, including support to armed groups and militias operating across the border, increasing the likelihood of retaliatory attacks and further regional destabilisation.

Over the next one to three months, further RSF incursions, SAF-backed proxy activity, or competition over border corridors could increase cross-border violence, displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad. Additional attacks or retaliations would likely worsen conditions in provinces already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees, further straining regional services, humanitarian operations, and community relations. The risk is not limited to humanitarian spillover and increasingly involves the possibility of sustained confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces.

text: The risk remains active, although no significant new cross-border attacks inside Chad were identified during the second half of September. Humanitarian pressure linked to the Sudan conflict has nevertheless increased sharply as fighting in Darfur and other parts of Sudan drives renewed displacement across the border. By 25 September, more than 400 Sudanese refugees were crossing into Chad each day, around 20 times the rate recorded in previous months, bringing arrivals since the beginning of 2026 to more than 55,000. The acceleration in arrivals is increasing pressure on already overstretched reception areas and services in eastern Chad, while funding constraints affect humanitarian organisations' capacity to provide shelter, food, and relocation assistance. Continued conflict in neighbouring Sudan therefore maintains the risk of further refugee arrivals and humanitarian deterioration in eastern Chad, while the potential for renewed cross-border security incidents remains, given the heightened military presence and tensions established along the border following the August strikes.

vulnerability: Before the Sudan conflict escalated, eastern Chad already faced high levels of poverty, food insecurity, weak infrastructure, and limited access to basic services. Refugee-hosting regions such as Ennedi Est, Ouaddai, Sila, and Wadi Fira have experienced sustained humanitarian pressure since 2023, with repeated refugee arrivals straining regional coping capacities, public services, and natural resources. Host communities in these areas also face chronic vulnerabilities linked to limited livelihood opportunities, climate shocks, water scarcity, and underdeveloped healthcare and education systems.

Insecurity, logistical challenges, and major funding gaps continue to constrain humanitarian response capacity. Several refugee-hosting areas depend heavily on humanitarian assistance, while overcrowded sites continue to face inadequate access to shelter, water, sanitation, healthcare, and protection services. Limited funding has already reduced food assistance and cash support in some locations, increasing reliance on potentially harmful coping mechanisms among refugees and host communities.

Protection risks are particularly high for women, children, and displaced populations. Overcrowding, limited lighting, long distances to water points, and weak service coverage increase exposure to gender-based violence, exploitation, and child protection risks. Repeated displacement and prolonged humanitarian needs have also reduced household resilience and increased tensions over access to resources and assistance in eastern Chad.
expected_impact: Further escalation of cross-border violence linked to the Sudan conflict could expose eastern Chad to new levels of civilian casualties, trauma, and insecurity. Additional drone strikes, shelling, armed incursions, or proxy attacks in border areas such as Adré, Tine, and the surrounding areas may directly affect civilians, trigger new displacement, and increase protection risks in communities already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees. Repeated exposure to violence and insecurity is also likely to increase psychological distress and trauma among affected populations.

Escalating military activity could damage or disrupt critical infrastructure, including transport routes, border facilities, health centres, markets, telecommunications infrastructure, and humanitarian supply corridors. Further insecurity along the Chad–Sudan border may reduce civilian mobility, restrict trade, and hinder humanitarian operations. If border crossings tighten or close, people fleeing violence in Darfur will find it more difficult to reach safety, and the delivery of humanitarian assistance and essential goods into eastern Chad will be limited.

Deteriorating security conditions may also increase public health risks. Displacement, overcrowding, disrupted health services, and reduced humanitarian access could contribute to disease outbreaks and weaken regional health systems’ response capacity. If violence expands or becomes sustained, humanitarian needs are likely to increase significantly across eastern Chad, particularly in border areas already facing limited service availability and weak coping capacities.

R1044.title: Forecast El Niño conditions threaten crop production and worsen food insecurity in Kenya

triggers.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September rainfall across western and northern Kenya
triggers.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing during May–July 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal JJAS rainfall across western and northern Kenya — where the unimodal long rains season in fact extends into August/September and has already tracked below average in April and early May — alongside above-normal temperatures. This combination is expected to reduce soil moisture during the critical grain-filling and maturation stages of long rains crops in the North Rift and western Kenya, directly threatening the October–November harvest. Pastoral areas across the ASALs are likely to experience accelerated rangeland deterioration and reduced water availability, compounding already fragile livestock recovery. Sources: ([ICPAC 19/05/2026](https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/)) Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 09-06-2026 Last update: 08-07-2026

triggers.title: El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December short rains season in eastern and coastal Kenya
triggers.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during Kenya's October–December short rains season, particularly across eastern and coastal areas. During the 2023 El Niño, wetter-than-normal OND conditions across eastern Kenya materialised as severe and damaging flooding. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, a comparable pattern of enhanced short rains is likely. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa. Should this materialise, flooding would damage infrastructure and cropland in areas already weakened by successive climate shocks, further compounding humanitarian needs heading into early 2027. Sources: ([ICPAC 22/08/2023](https://www.icpac.net/news/october-to-december-2023-seasonal-forecast-el-ni%C3%B1o-climate-phenomenon-will-likely-bring-heavy-rains-across-the-greater-horn-of-africa/)) Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 09-06-2026 Last update: 08-07-2026

rationale: El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya.

The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. Combined with delayed fertiliser deliveries, below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures from June–September are likely to reduce yields of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato, resulting in a below-average October–November harvest.

In northern and eastern pastoral areas, above-average temperatures during the June–September dry season are expected to accelerate the deterioration of rangeland and water resources. Recovery remains fragile after the 2020–2023 drought and the 2023–2024 floods, with depleted herd sizes, persistent livestock disease, and reduced vaccination programmes limiting resilience.

The deteriorating production outlook comes as maize and bean prices remain 6–21% and 8–17% above the five-year average, respectively, driven by depleted household stocks following the poor 2025 short rains, high transport costs, and strong market demand. High household debt further constrains purchasing power. A below-average harvest would tighten domestic food supplies, drive prices higher, and further reduce incomes and food access for farming and pastoral households.

text: El Niño has driven a dry spell that has cut Kenya's harvest and is now expected to bring above-average short rains and flooding, with Lamu county projected to reach Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Dadaab camp Emergency (IPC Phase 4) between October–January. The dry spell caused a poor long rains harvest, with maize production estimated at 22–28% below the five-year average and losses of up to 43% anticipated in high potential North Rift counties including Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu, and Nakuru. The Ministry of Agriculture has acknowledged widespread crop failure in the North Rift, which produces over 60% of Kenya's maize. Wholesale maize prices in Nairobi are expected to remain 9–19% above the five-year average until January 2027, limiting food access for poor households. The October–December rains are expected to improve pastoral conditions, but in Dadaab flooding is likely to last for weeks, limiting humanitarian access and increasing waterborne disease. IPC 3 outcomes are expected to persist in Garissa, Mandera, Tana River, Wajir, and Turkana counties through January, where flooding is likely to damage transport infrastructure and displace households. A national assessment has identified 18 counties and 5,660 health facilities in areas at risk of flooding.

vulnerability: Kenya's arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs), home to the majority of pastoral and agropastoral communities, are characterised by chronic food insecurity and structural dependence on livestock and rain-fed agriculture. The 2020–2023 La Niña drought and the 2023–2024 El Niño flooding have left household asset bases severely depleted, with herd sizes yet to recover and debt levels constraining investment in the current growing season. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity levels have persisted across pastoral areas, with the situation not expected to improve before September 2026. The North Rift and western Kenya, the country’s principal maize- and bean-growing regions (with the planting season in March and harvest typically from October–November) have little buffer against a poor season, as a shortfall there reduces food availability nationally, not only locally.

Market conditions offer little buffer. Staple food prices remain above average, purchasing power is eroded by rising fuel and transport costs, and fertiliser shortages are already affecting input use ahead of the critical JJAS growing period. Reduced humanitarian funding has left many host community households without adequate support.

Over 720,000 refugees in Dadaab, Kakuma, and Kalobeyei settlements face IPC 3 conditions. While food assistance has partially mitigated the most severe outcomes, current ration levels remain insufficient to meet minimum food needs across all households, and the ability to respond to further deterioration is constrained.
expected_impact: Below-average JJAS precipitation and above-average temperatures would directly threaten the October–November harvest of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato across the North Rift and western Kenya – crops that represent the primary source of domestic food production. Reduced yields would tighten household food stocks at a time when they are already depleted, drive staple prices higher in already-stressed markets, and erode incomes for farming households with limited capacity to cope. In pastoral areas, accelerated rangeland deterioration and reduced water availability from June onwards would increase livestock mortality and reduce milk output, deepening food insecurity across the ASALs. IPC 3 outcomes, already widespread, are likely to expand in geographic scope and severity, with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) a credible risk in the most exposed pastoral counties. Acute malnutrition among children and pregnant and lactating women – already above emergency thresholds in refugee camps – is likely to worsen across both pastoral and camp populations as food access declines.

Should El Niño enhance the October–December short rains as forecast precedent suggests, eastern and coastal Kenya face a contrasting but equally damaging set of impacts. Flooding would damage standing crops, destroy infrastructure, and disrupt market supply chains at a critical point in the post-harvest period. Displacement from flood-affected areas would increase pressure on host communities and services already under strain. During the October 2023 to January 2024 El Niño short rains, at least 178 people died, and thousands of households were displaced.

Across both hazards, the response capacity will be constrained. Humanitarian funding gaps, reduced food ration levels, and limited government reach into remote pastoral and flood-affected areas mean that rising needs are unlikely to be fully met. If both the JJAS drought and October–December flooding materialise, Kenya faces a sustained deterioration in humanitarian conditions through the end of 2026 and into early 2027.

R1045.title: Forecast below-average Kiremt rains in Ethiopia threaten food production and livelihoods

triggers.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia's key Meher-producing areas
triggers.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing by 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with precipitation deficits likely in the northeastern and central areas, where there is at least a 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more. This combination of reduced rainfall and above average temperatures during the critical Kiremt season is expected to suppress Meher crop yields, reduce agricultural labour demand, and accelerate pasture and water scarcity in pastoral areas. Sources: ([ICPAC 19/05/2026](https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/)) Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 09-06-2026 Last update: 08-07-2026

triggers.title: Strengthening El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December season in lowland and riverine areas of Ethiopia
triggers.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during the October–December season across eastern East Africa. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, there is an increased likelihood of flooding across flood-prone lowland areas of Ethiopia, especially the Somali Region. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa. Sources: ([FEWS NET Seasonal Monitor 27/05/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/seasonal-monitor/may-2026)) Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 09-06-2026 Last update: 08-07-2026

rationale: El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration puts the probability of El Niño from May–July at around 61%, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre's May 2026 forecast indicates a high likelihood of below-normal June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with above-normal temperatures. Severe localised deficits are likely in the northeast and central areas, with at least 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more.

Kiremt is the primary rainy season for Ethiopia's northern and central cropping areas, governing the Meher harvest – the country's most important crop season, which produces the most teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley across Amhara, Central Ethiopia, Oromia, the Southern regions, and Tigray. Below-average rainfall would cut yields and household food production. In Tigray and Amhara, poor rains may also reduce agricultural labour income during the June–August lean season.

In past El Niño episodes, Meher maize and sorghum production fell across Ethiopia, most sharply in eastern Amhara,  northeastern Oromia, and Tigray; national yields dropped by around 2% below normal, with localised deficits of 10–15%. High fertiliser and fuel prices will likely limit farmers' input use during planting, lowering yield potential even with adequate rainfall, while raising transport costs for inputs and produce.

Staple food prices are already exceptionally high; annual food inflation reached 13.5% in April, up from 11% in March but down from 15.6% in April 2025 – a renewed monthly acceleration after disinflation, not a sustained year-on-year worsening. Drivers include increased fuel costs from Middle East conflict-linked energy disruptions, seasonal lean season food supply tightening, and trade disruptions, which are severely straining poor rural households.

El Niño typically also boosts the October–December rainfall across lowland/riverine eastern East Africa. Forecasts show a very high chance of above-average rainfall across central and eastern Ethiopia, likely driving flooding in flood-prone lowlands. (,,,,, [WMO accessed 08/07/2026](wmolc.org/seasonPmmeUI/view?winName=PlotView1781162850270))

text: The risk remained stable in September, with conditions continuing to follow the drought-then-flood pattern expected under El Niño. Rainfall deficits during the June–September Kiremt rains exceeded 50% of average across much of the country, and the Meher harvest, which provides over 85% of national crop production, could be up to 30% below average, with the worst-affected areas being Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar, and eastern Oromia regions. Slight late-season improvements in rainfall are unlikely to help earlier planted crops substantially, although later planted crops may benefit. In northeastern pastoral areas, deficits have rapidly depleted surface water and increased distances to watering points, while pasture in the southeast is deteriorating after the rains ended. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist through January 2027 across many drought-affected areas, with some households facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4). October–December rainfall is forecast to be above average, with up to a 90% probability of enhanced rainfall in southern Ethiopia. In September, the Ethiopian Meteorological Institute warned of flash flooding and landslides in southwestern, southern, and southeastern lowlands, with rainfall up to 75% above normal in parts of the south. The institute also cautioned that unseasonal rains in northern, northeastern, and eastern areas could damage mature crops ready for harvest, meaning drought and flood impacts could occur at the same time in different parts of the country.

vulnerability: Ethiopia's rural population – the majority of whom depend on agriculture for their food and income – is highly vulnerable to climate shocks. The 2020–2023 drought and a further poor season in 2025 have left pastoral and agropastoral households in the south and southeast with depleted herd sizes and limited capacity to absorb a further climatic shock. In the northern and central cropping areas, households are entering the Kiremt season with already constrained food stocks, with Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity outcomes widespread and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) levels persisting in the East Hararghe lowlands since February 2026. In Central Ethiopia, Oromia, and Tigray, delayed Belg rains led to a significant reduction in planted areas by April. Conflict in Amhara continues to disrupt markets, livelihoods, and transport routes, compounding climate-related vulnerability and constraining households' ability to cope with further shocks. The country's heavy dependence on imported fuel and fertiliser exposes households to global price volatility, further eroding purchasing power. While data availability remains limited, registered refugees across the country face IPC 3 outcomes, relying on humanitarian assistance and limited livelihood activities – meaning the population entering the June–September Kiremt season has severely limited capacity to cope with below-average rainfall.
expected_impact: Below-average Kiremt rainfall would directly reduce Meher crop yields across Ethiopia's northern and central highlands, where teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley are the primary staples. Reduced production would tighten household food stocks ahead of the post-harvest period, drive staple prices higher in already severely stressed markets, and eliminate the seasonal agricultural labour opportunities that poor rural households depend on for income during the lean season. In the pastoral south and southeast, accelerated pasture and water scarcity from June onwards would drive livestock migration, increase mortality rates, and further suppress milk availability – deepening food insecurity in areas where IPC 3 is already widespread and herd recovery from successive droughts remains incomplete. A poor Kiremt season would likely push significant numbers of households currently in IPC 3 into IPC 4, with the most exposed areas being the northeastern and central highlands, where rainfall deficits are forecast to be most severe, and the eastern pastoral zones of Somali region.

Should El Niño enhance the October–December rains as forecast precedent suggests, flood-prone lowland areas of Ethiopia face a contrasting but equally damaging set of impacts. Flooding would damage infrastructure, displace communities, and disrupt market supply chains at a time when households are already weakened by a poor Kiremt season.

Across both hazards, limited data availability, elevated humanitarian funding gaps, and access challenges in parts of the country severely constrain the response capacity. If both the Kiremt drought and October–December flooding materialise, Ethiopia faces a sustained and deepening deterioration in humanitarian conditions through the end of 2026 and into early 2027.

R1046.title: El Niño drives drought conditions, increasing food insecurity and heightening humanitarian needs in Madagascar in 2027

triggers.title: Rainfall deficits and above average precipitation affecting agricultural production
triggers.description: Dry conditions are likely to lead to reduced soil moisture, crop failure, and declining pasture availability, which in turn limit household food production and income from agriculture. This reduces food availability at the household level and increases reliance on markets at a time of constrained purchasing power. Sources: (Moov 03/06/2026 ; Meteomadagascar 29/04/2026 ; FEWS NET 05/06/2026 ; OCHA 30/04/2026 ; UNRIC 21/04/2026) Completion rate: 60% Completion rate history: 19-06-2026: 50% 07-08-2026: 60% 05-10-2026: 60% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Deteriorated Trend history: 07-08-2026: Deteriorated 05-10-2026: Deteriorated Date entered: 19-06-2026 Last update: 05-10-2026

rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. In 2015–2016 and 2023–2024, El Niño caused prolonged drought conditions and crop failure, resulting in increased food insecurity that particularly affected the country's south. Seasonal forecasts anticipate near-average precipitation in July–September and below-average precipitation across most of the country in October–December. The same forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average temperatures across the entire country in July–December. Drier and hotter-than-average conditions may affect the start of the rainy season, which runs October–April and is essential for producing Madagascar's main staple cereals, such as maize and rice, harvested in April–June. This may lead to below-average yields, with severe consequences for the population's access to food in 2027, widening food consumption gaps and increasing malnutrition rates. Impacts may also extend to other staple crops, such as cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, as well as to agricultural labour availability, which usually peaks between November–March. Limited rainfall and abnormally high temperatures may also reduce pasture availability, resulting in deteriorating livestock body conditions and increased morbidity and mortality. Dry conditions are also likely to affect access to water for domestic consumption, potentially leading to reliance on unsafe water sources and limiting hygiene and sanitation practices. These combined effects are expected to increase humanitarian needs, strain local coping mechanisms, and heighten dependence on external assistance, particularly among rural households already vulnerable to climate variability. The country shows a high pre-existing vulnerability to climatic shocks, including reliance on rainfed agriculture, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, and low coping capacity.

text: The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Assessments indicate that the lean season has already started earlier than usual in the Grand South, with poor households exhausting food stocks in September following below-average 2025/26 harvests and increasingly relying on markets and negative coping strategies. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). El Niño-related rainfall deficits could further reduce 2027 crop production and household incomes, particularly in the Grand South, increasing food insecurity and humanitarian needs through early 2027, though past El Niño events had limited effects on national paddy output.

vulnerability: Madagascar faces high structural vulnerability, with extreme poverty estimated at around 65% in April 2026, limiting households' ability to absorb shocks. Livelihoods are largely dependent on rainfed agriculture, making them highly sensitive to climate variability. Recurrent climatic shocks continue to erode resilience, as demonstrated by the cyclones Fytia and Gezani in early 2026, which affected nearly 700,000 people, damaging homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Food security conditions remain fragile. During the February–April 2026 period, an estimated 1.8 million people were expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes, with limited access to food and income. In southwestern Madagascar, persistent rainfall shortages since the start of the rainy season in October 2025 have limited agricultural production. Field assessments conducted in early May 2026 confirmed maize and pulse yields below average for the typical May harvest period. Local markets also showed unusually low supplies of maize and cassava. Coping capacity is further constrained by worsening malnutrition levels, with around 558,000 children under five either affected or at risk of acute malnutrition between May 2025 and April 2026. Many households are already employing coping mechanisms with potentially harmful consequences, including reducing food intake, selling productive assets, or taking on debt. Repeated exposure to shocks, combined with limited access to services and weak infrastructure, continues to reduce households' ability to recover, increasing dependence on humanitarian assistance. (, [IFRC 16/04/2026]( https://reliefweb.int/report/madagascar/madagascar-2026-cyclones-operation-update-2-mdrmg027),, )
expected_impact: The effects of El Niño-induced drought are expected to result in deteriorating food security, increased malnutrition, and heightened humanitarian needs. In the south, rainfall deficits are likely to lead to the most severe impacts, as the region already experiences prolonged dry conditions and a poor 2025–2026 rainy season. Across the country, similarly poor conditions in 2026–2027 may lead to reduced agricultural production, depletion of household food stocks, and increased reliance on markets, where purchasing power remains constrained because of poverty and limited income opportunities. This is expected to widen food consumption gaps, particularly among rural households dependent on rainfed agriculture. El Niño is also expected to significantly affect WASH conditions and public health. In southern areas, water scarcity will likely reduce access to safe drinking water and hygiene services. This is critical given that only about 36% of the rural population has access to improved water sources, and only around 10% use basic sanitation facilities, leaving many communities highly exposed to water shortages and unsafe practices. In contrast, above-average rainfall and cyclones in the north and east during El Niño periods can lead to flooding, contaminating water sources and increasing the spread of waterborne and vector-borne diseases such as cholera and malaria. Poor WASH access already contributes significantly to child mortality and illness. Across affected areas, pre-existing vulnerabilities such as high poverty, limited coping capacity, and weak infrastructure are likely to amplify the impact of these shocks. Malnutrition risks are expected to increase, particularly among children under five, driven by reduced food availability and access and deteriorated access to water, sanitation, and hygiene. At the same time, repeated shocks are likely to further erode households' coping strategies, pushing them to adopt coping mechanisms with potentially harmful consequences, including reducing food intake and selling productive assets. (, [IFRC 16/04/2026]( https://reliefweb.int/report/madagascar/madagascar-2026-cyclones-operation-update-2-mdrmg027),,,,,,,,,,,, )

R1047.title: El Niño-induced dry conditions in southern and central Mozambique and floods in the northern provinces increase humanitarian needs in 2026 and early 2027

triggers.title: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions
triggers.description: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions: During El Niño events, large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts suppress moisture transport into southern Africa, reducing rainfall during the main cropping season. In southern and central Mozambique, this often results in prolonged dry spells, erratic rainfall distribution, and early cessation of rains rather than a complete absence of precipitation. At the same time, above-average temperatures increase evapotranspiration rates, accelerating the loss of soil moisture and surface water. This combination reduces water availability for domestic consumption, crops and livestock, heightens the risk of pasture degradation, and can lead to reduced agricultural yields or crop failure, particularly for rainfed smallholder farmers. Sources: (Afroline 17/05/2026 ; CoM 18/05/2026 ; FEWS NET 21/05/2026 ; WMO 02/06/2026 ; IRI accessed 11/06/2026) Completion rate: 60% Completion rate history: 19-06-2026: 50% 07-08-2026: 60% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Deteriorated Trend history: 07-08-2026: Deteriorated Date entered: 19-06-2026 Last update: 07-08-2026

triggers.title: Above-average rainfall in northern provinces
triggers.description: El Niño conditions can enhance moisture inflow in parts of northern Mozambique, leading to above-average and more intense rainfall events. This increases the likelihood of river overflow, flash floods, and waterlogging, especially in low-lying and flood-prone districts. Saturated soils reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff, amplifying flood severity even during short periods of heavy rainfall. Flooding can damage homes, crops, and transport infrastructure, disrupt market access, and increase the risk of population displacement and waterborne diseases, further compounding humanitarian needs. Sources: (Afroline 17/05/2026 ; CoM 18/05/2026 ; FEWS NET 21/05/2026 ; WMO 02/06/2026) Completion rate: 50% Completion rate history: 19-06-2026: 50% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Stable Trend history: 07-08-2026: Stable Date entered: 19-06-2026 Last update: 07-08-2026

triggers.title: Delayed onset and irregular distribution of rains
triggers.description: El Niño is often associated with a late or erratic start to the rainy season, followed by uneven rainfall patterns throughout the season. In Mozambique, this disrupts the agricultural calendar, delaying planting and reducing the effective growing period for key crops such as maize. Intermittent dry spells during critical crop growth stages can further reduce yields. At the same time, unpredictable rainfall undermines farmers’ decision-making and increases the likelihood of replanting, leading to higher input costs and reduced resilience among households dependent on farming. Sources: (Afroline 17/05/2026 ; CoM 18/05/2026 ; FEWS NET 21/05/2026 ; WMO 02/06/2026) Completion rate: 60% Completion rate history: 19-06-2026: 50% 05-10-2026: 60% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Deteriorated Trend history: 07-08-2026: Stable 05-10-2026: Deteriorated Date entered: 19-06-2026 Last update: 05-10-2026

rationale: Climate projections indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions developing in July 2026 and persisting into the 2026/2027 rainy season, coinciding with Mozambique's main agricultural period. El Niño will drive contrasting rainfall patterns, with drier conditions in southern and central regions and wetter conditions in the north. The anticipated event is driven by abnormal warming of equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures, which disrupts global atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. El Niño typically brings below-normal rains in southern Mozambique and above-normal rains to the northern provinces, raising the likelihood of flooding and river overflow. Seasonal forecasts for the October–December period anticipate these typical El Niño patterns, indicating a moderate probability of above-average precipitation in the north and below-average precipitation in the south. The entire country is expected to experience above-average temperatures in July–December, which will compound dry conditions in the south and increase the risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases in flood-exposed areas. Mozambique's high exposure to climate variability and reliance on rainfed agriculture further amplify vulnerability to climatic shocks. From September–October 2026, delayed or below-average precipitation in southern and central areas, combined with abnormally high temperatures, may affect land preparation and planting. If dry conditions continue through early 2027, crop yields and water availability may decrease, leading to a below-average maize, rice, millet, and sorghum harvest. At the same time, northern areas are likely to experience above-average precipitation, which may be beneficial to agriculture but also increases the risk of flooding, infrastructure damage, and displacement. These combined impacts are expected to increase humanitarian needs, particularly in food security, nutrition, WASH, and health. (, [FEWS NET accessed 11/06/2026]( https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique),, [WMO 24/04/2026] (https://wmo.int/media/news/wmo-likelihood-increases-of-el-nino),,, )

text: The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Assessments indicate that the lean season has already started earlier than usual in the Grand South, with poor households exhausting food stocks in September following below-average 2025/26 harvests and increasingly relying on markets and negative coping strategies. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). El Niño-related rainfall deficits could further reduce 2027 crop production and household incomes, particularly in the Grand South, increasing food insecurity and humanitarian needs through early 2027, though past El Niño events had limited effects on national paddy output.

vulnerability: Mozambique faces a challenging humanitarian situation marked by overlapping health, conflict, and climate shocks. A cholera outbreak that began in September 2025 continues in 2026, with over 9,000 cases reported and the highest transmission in Nampula, Tete, and Cabo Delgado provinces by the end of May 2026. Limited access to safe water and sanitation, particularly in flood-prone and densely populated areas, continues to facilitate transmission and strain already fragile health services. At the same time, the insurgency in northern Mozambique, active since October 2017, continues to drive displacement and disrupt livelihoods, particularly in Cabo Delgado, with spillover into Nampula and Niassa. Recurrent attacks and insecurity have displaced hundreds of thousands of people, many of whom remain dependent on humanitarian assistance and have limited access to land and basic services. Recent flooding during the 2025/2026 rainy season further weakened coping capacity, with over 1 million people affected, mostly in central and southern provinces. Flood damage to infrastructure, crops, and livelihoods has reduced household resilience and increased reliance on assistance. Overall, repeated shocks, widespread poverty, and dependence on rainfed agriculture have eroded coping capacities, leaving these populations highly exposed to additional climate-related hazards. (,,,, [INGD accessed 11/06/2026]( https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/cenoe/viz/DASHBOARD_IMPACTO_INGD_EXTERNO_17418596149660/Dashboard),, )
expected_impact: The anticipated El Niño during the 2026/2027 rainy season is expected to generate significant multisector humanitarian impacts across Mozambique, consistent with impacts observed during the 2023/2024 El Niño event. During that period, below-average rainfall and high temperatures in southern and central regions led to widespread drought, crop failure, and declining agricultural production, with national output losses and reduced yields concentrated in central and southern provinces. These conditions contributed to large-scale food insecurity, with up to 4.9 million people facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse conditions by early 2025. Similar patterns are expected in 2026/2027, with reduced rainfall and rising temperatures likely to limit soil moisture, reduce crop yields, and constrain water availability, particularly for subsistence households reliant on rainfed agriculture. This will likely translate into reduced food access, income losses, and increased malnutrition risk. Conversely, during the 2023/2024 El Niño, northern Mozambique experienced above-average rainfall and localised flooding, damaging crops and infrastructure and disrupting livelihoods. A similar flood risk is expected in northern provinces in 2026/2027, potentially causing infrastructure damage, market disruption, and heightened risk of waterborne diseases, including cholera. Impacts will likely be amplified in conflict-affected northern areas (Cabo Delgado, Nampula, Niassa), where displacement and limited access to services reduce coping capacity. Overall, El Niño is likely to simultaneously drive drought in the south and flooding in the north, increasing humanitarian needs across food security, WASH, health, and livelihoods, with the most severe impacts during the peak rainy season. (,,,,,,, [WMO 24/04/2026] (https://wmo.int/media/news/wmo-likelihood-increases-of-el-nino),,,,,, )

R1048.title: RSF expansion in Blue Nile state triggers displacement and protection risks

triggers.title: RSF advances north from Baw
triggers.description: RSF movement towards Ed Damazine or the Roseires Dam corridor would indicate expansion beyond current front lines and increase displacement risk. Sources: ([ACLED 26/01/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/blue-nile-peripheral-front-central-battleground-sudan-conflict), [MEE 26/01/2026](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/sudans-rsf-launches-offensive-blue-nile-state), [AJ 19/08/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longform/2025/8/19/inside-the-nuba-mountains-and-the-alliance-reshaping-sudans-civil-war), [ACLED 15/04/2025](https://acleddata.com/report/two-years-war-sudan-how-saf-gaining-upper-hand), [ICG 07/04/2025](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/sudan/two-years-sudans-war-spreading), [Reuters 10/02/2026](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/ethiopia-builds-secret-camp-train-sudan-rsf-fighters-sources-say-2026-02-10/)) Completion rate: 40% Completion rate history: 19-06-2026: 80% 19-06-2026: 40% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 19-06-2026 Last update: 19-06-2026

triggers.description: Arming, inflammatory messaging, or clashes among communities affected by displacement and resource pressure would raise protection risks. Sources: ([ST 05/02/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/310285), [WVI 05/02/2026](https://www.wvi.org/stories/sudan/world-vision-supports-displaced-families-tadamon-locality), [Protection Cluster 03/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/protection-alert-blue-nile-state-sudan-2-april-2026), [Protection Cluster 02/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/sudan-protection-cluster-alert-blue-nile-2-april-2026), [IOM 28/10/2022](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/iom-sudan-displacement-tracking-matrixdtm-sudan-ar-rusayris-blue-nile-update-8-28-october-2022)) Completion rate: 30% Completion rate history: 19-06-2026: 30% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 19-06-2026 Last update: 19-06-2026

rationale: The RSF offensive launched in early 2026 against Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) positions in Baw county opened a new front in Blue Nile state. This has significantly increased the likelihood of conflict spreading to previously unaffected areas to the north, particularly Ed Damazine, the state capital, as well as the strategic corridor leading to the Roseires Dam. By advancing in Blue Nile state, RSF seeks to strengthen its position to recapture and control central Sudan, later opening a route through Sennar state.

Following heavy territorial losses in 2025, including entire states in central Sudan, RSF has reconstituted its operational capacity through its alliance with Abdelaziz Adam al Hilu's Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N/Al Hilu). Access to terrain under its control has provided RSF with defensive depth, cross-border supply lines, and logistical continuity. This enables it to sustain multifront operations and power its advance in Blue Nile, positioning the RSF for a prolonged and expanded offensive rather than a short-term tactical push and increasing the likelihood of escalation beyond the current front lines.

External facilitation further compounds these dynamics. SAF has repeatedly accused South Sudan and Ethiopia of enabling this mobilisation, with satellite imagery from February 2026 showing a logistics camp near the Ethiopian border in Benishangul Gumz despite official Ethiopian denial. If sustained, such external support would significantly raise the possibility of a scaled-up offensive by insulating RSF operations from battlefield setbacks ([ACLED 26/01/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/blue-nile-peripheral-front-central-battleground-sudan-conflict ),, [AJ 19/08/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longform/2025/8/19/inside-the-nuba-mountains-and-the-alliance-reshaping-sudans-civil-war ),,, [Reuters 10/02/2026](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/ethiopia-builds-secret-camp-train-sudan-rsf-fighters-sources-say-2026-02-10/ ), )

text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) expanded their territorial control in Blue Nile. On 11 August, the alliance captured Geisan, followed by Al Kurmuk on 13 August, after the Sudanese Armed Forces withdrew from the town. The offensive triggered significant displacement; more than 5,000 people had reached Ed Damazine by 18 August, while IOM reported nearly 14,000 displaced from Geisan and Al Kurmuk throughout the month. By 28 August, RSF and SPLM-N had claimed control of Bakori and Surkum military bases, while satellite analysis identified around 100 additional light technical vehicles at an Ethiopian base near Assosa, indicating preparations for further advances towards Ed Damazine. (, [AJ 13/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/13/sudan-army-says-rsf-advance-on-key-town-bordering-ethiopia],,, ).

vulnerability: Blue Nile has limited capacity to absorb another escalation. Recent clashes in At Tadamon and Baw have already displaced large numbers of people into areas where shelter, safe water, sanitation, health, and protection services are under pressure. Ed Damazine and surrounding towns are hosting newly displaced people while also serving resident populations affected by inflation, insecurity, and reduced livelihoods. Newly displaced households, women, children, older people, and people with disabilities are likely to have weaker coping capacity because displacement disrupts income, social networks, and access to assistance. Ethnic diversity, including Ingessana, Berta, and Hamaj communities, increases sensitivity to resource competition and politicised narratives around population movements. Host communities may also face pressure as land, water, services, and livelihood opportunities become more constrained.
expected_impact: If fighting expands north, large-scale displacement is likely towards Ed Damazine, other urban centres in northern Blue Nile, and neighbouring states. Newly displaced households would likely arrive with limited assets, increasing demand for emergency shelter, NFIs, safe water, sanitation, health services, and protection support. Overcrowding in informal settlements and host communities would heighten the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly where water and sanitation infrastructure is already weak. Fighting in populated areas, including drone strikes or shelling, could damage health, water, power, and road infrastructure, further reducing service availability and humanitarian access. Protection risks would likely increase, including family separation, GBV, child protection violations, psychosocial distress, and targeted violence against communities perceived as aligned with armed or political actors. Competition over land, livelihoods, and basic services could also trigger or worsen intercommunal tensions, particularly if displacement is framed as altering local power dynamics.

R1049.title: RSF restoration of siege on Al Obeid, North Kordofan drives widescale displacement towards White Nile state

rationale: Since October 2025, RSF has mobilised troops near Al Obeid's borders, including deploying combat vehicles along the western side. The sustained mobilisation and positioning of these forces indicate preparation for a renewed offensive to reinstate a siege of the city. A previous siege of the city between May 2023 and February 2025 demonstrated RSF's operational ability to isolate Al Obeid for prolonged periods, resulting in a significant deterioration in humanitarian conditions, including severe food insecurity.

RSF has a strong strategic incentive to restore the siege because of Al Obeid's role as a key logistic and commercial hub linking western and southern Sudan to Khartoum and central Sudan. Control of the city would provide RSF with greater leverage over supply routes, trade flows, and access to corridors into SAF-controlled areas, particularly central Sudan. Al Obeid's role as a major crop and livestock market and a gate for Kordofan exports further increases its strategic and economic importance to RSF.

Despite recent SAF advancements and repositioning in North Kordofan, fluid conflict dynamics and continued shifts in areas of control between SAF and RSF increase the likelihood of renewed attempts to siege the city over the next six months. This likelihood is further reinforced by increasing logistical and technical support provided to RSF by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which may improve the group's operational capacity to sustain offensive and siege tactics.

text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) intensified around Al Obeid city, North Kordofan state. On 12 August, suspected RSF drones struck the city, killing two people and injuring others. From 14–15 August, RSF attacks on Um Arda locality, Tamid village, and Al Khor Al Abyad village, North Kordofan state, displaced 4,250 people; the attack on Um Arda alone killed 18 civilians and displaced more than 300 families towards Al Obeid. On 20 August, RSF attacks on Um Dareisa village and Al Shaqla village, North Kordofan state, killed six civilians and displaced more than 1,000 people towards Al Obeid city. These attacks increased pressure on the city and advanced the siege and displacement pathways of the risk..

vulnerability: Al Obeid is highly vulnerable because it already functions as a displacement hub and market centre for conflict-affected populations from South and West Kordofan. North Kordofan hosts more than 2.3 million displaced people, increasing pressure on shelter, services, markets, and host communities. The city already faces inflation in essential commodities, particularly food and fuel, because of disrupted and inconsistent supply chains. Household coping capacity is weak, especially among IDPs who have limited livelihood opportunities, limited savings, and high dependence on markets or assistance. Health capacity is also fragile: one of the few functioning public hospitals in the state is receiving patients from neighbouring conflict-affected areas while managing mass casualty incidents and outbreaks such as dengue fever and cholera. Renewed siege conditions would therefore affect populations already facing overlapping displacement, food insecurity, health, and access constraints.
expected_impact: A renewed RSF siege on Al Obeid could trigger large primary and secondary displacement, particularly among people already displaced from South and West Kordofan. Many households would likely move towards White Nile, especially Kosti, which remains linked by transport routes and has previously attracted people fleeing conflict in Kordofan. Movement restrictions, fear of ground assault, market disruption, and deteriorating living conditions would likely drive further departures. Inside Al Obeid, siege conditions would reduce access to food, fuel, medicines, markets, health services, and humanitarian assistance. Shortages and sharp price increases would weaken purchasing power and worsen food insecurity among residents, IDPs, and host communities. Because Al Obeid is a major agricultural and commercial market connecting Greater Darfur with eastern and northern Sudan, prolonged disruption could also affect wider trade flows and commodity availability across Kordofan and Darfur. Health impacts would include reduced medical supply delivery, strain on hospital capacity, and weaker outbreak response for cholera, dengue fever, and other diseases.

rationale: The continuation or expansion of trade bans imposed in late 2025 by Khartoum, Northern, and North Kordofan states on the movement of goods into RSF-controlled areas would likely further restrict supplies to West Kordofan. These restrictions would affect food, fuel, medicines, agricultural inputs, and other essential commodities. West Kordofan is particularly exposed because it is landlocked and has historically depended on supply chains from northern and eastern Sudan, including routes through Khartoum, Red Sea ports, and Egypt. As formal routes become more restricted, markets are likely to rely increasingly on informal supply routes that are longer, more insecure, and more expensive because of checkpoints, unofficial taxation, transport delays, and insecurity. Alternative routes through Al Na'am market near Abyei provide some supply capacity but are limited and vulnerable to shocks, including fires, border tensions, and armed-party interference. If bans persist, supply shortages and price increases are likely to deepen food insecurity and market fragmentation across the state.

text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as restrictions on trade routes and markets increasingly constrained food availability and affordability in West Kordofan. On 6 August, Northern state authorities tightened controls on commercial trucks travelling towards Kordofan and Darfur, confiscating two trucks carrying food and fuel; millet reached SSP 900,000 per sack and onions SSP 2 million in An Nuhud locality, West Kordofan. By 15 August, households were consuming ambaz, an animal-feed byproduct, amid unaffordable food prices. On 26 August, authorities of the Rapid Support Forces closed public markets, restricted movement, and shut down Starlink services in An Nuhud, further disrupting commercial activity and food access. Although Khartoum state had reopened the export route on 14 August, continued restrictions elsewhere compounded market disruption. ([Darfur24 26/08/2026](https://darfur24.com/en/2026/08/06/northern-state-tightens-ban-on-goods-bound-for-kordofan],,, ).

vulnerability: West Kordofan already has high vulnerability because food insecurity, conflict, market disruption, and weak service access overlap. IPC projected more than one million people, around 46% of the state population, to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between February-May 2026, with Lagawa and As Sunut facing famine risk. Households are already affected by inflation, currency depreciation, cash shortages, and reduced income opportunities. Coping capacity is low, especially for poor rural households, IDPs, pastoralists, and market-dependent communities that rely on increasingly expensive food, fuel, medicine, seeds, and veterinary inputs. Disrupted agricultural inputs and limited access to vaccination for humans and livestock increase livelihood and health risks. Protection risks may also increase as families adopt harmful coping strategies, including reducing meals, selling productive assets, early marriage, or movement in search of food and services.
expected_impact: Continued trade restrictions would reduce the availability of food, fuel, medicines, seeds, machinery, and other essential commodities in West Kordofan. Transport and transaction costs would likely increase and be passed on to consumers through higher prices, further reducing household purchasing power. Food insecurity would deepen as households face lower dietary diversity, reduced meal frequency, and less access to affordable staple foods. Limited agricultural inputs could undermine cultivation and reduce future harvests, while disrupted human and veterinary vaccination could increase disease risks and affect livestock productivity, livelihoods, and food availability. Rising food and fuel prices would likely also reduce access to health services, water trucking, transport, and humanitarian assistance. Households facing severe shortages may increasingly use harmful coping strategies, including consuming seeds reserved for planting, selling productive assets, and taking on debt. Deteriorating conditions could drive further displacement from rural and conflict-affected areas towards urban centres or assistance locations, increasing pressure on services and potentially worsening IPC Phase 5 risks in famine-risk localities.

rationale: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) face growing pressure from key external allies, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the US, to distance itself from allied armed groups with political Islam leanings, including the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. This creates a risk of fragmentation within SAF's alliance structure, as attempts to contain, integrate, or undermine these groups could provoke resistance. SAF remains operationally dependent on allied armed groups for manpower, mobilisation, funding channels, and battlefield capacity across multiple fronts, making coercive integration difficult. Tensions have also emerged between SAF and factions linked to JEM, the Joint Forces, and other groups present in civilian and commercial areas in Khartoum. US designation and sanctions linked to the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood and Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade add further external pressure on SAF to disengage from these groups. If SAF pursues integration or restrictions while these actors retain military leverage and local positions, tensions could escalate into localised clashes, checkpoint competition, and fragmented territorial control in Khartoum and central Sudan.

text: The risk remained stable during July 2026, with no clear public reporting of open clashes between SAF and its allied armed groups in Khartoum. The underlying drivers of the risk remained present. External pressure on SAF to distance itself from armed groups with political Islamist leanings continued in the background, following the earlier designation and sanctions targeting the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. The brigade continued to play an important role in SAF-aligned mobilisation, with links to Islamist networks and alleged ties to Iranian support, sustaining the potential for friction between SAF's military dependence on allied groups and external pressure to contain them. At the same time, developments in July centred more on drone strikes, the escalation in Kordofan, and RSF external support networks than on fragmentation among SAF-aligned groups in Khartoum. The risk therefore remains active but has not clearly moved closer to materialisation during July.

vulnerability: Khartoum remains highly vulnerable despite efforts to encourage returns and reopen state institutions. Many areas continue to face damaged infrastructure, limited health and WASH services, disrupted markets, insecurity, and weak public-service capacity. Returnees, IDPs, poor urban households, women, children, and people living near strategic installations or markets would be particularly exposed if fighting resumes. Coping capacity is limited because many households have already exhausted savings, lost livelihoods, and rely on fragile markets or community support. Humanitarian responders also face high access constraints, including insecurity, checkpoints, fragmented authority, and risks to aid convoys, warehouses, hospitals, and staff. Local civil society and mutual aid groups may remain essential because of their community embeddedness, but they could face additional pressure if territorial control fragments further.
expected_impact: A rift between SAF and allied armed groups could trigger localised fighting around garrisons, military headquarters, markets, logistical infrastructure, and key transport corridors in Khartoum. Even if clashes remain localised, they could fragment areas of control and create parallel checkpoints, disrupting commercial goods, humanitarian assistance, fuel supplies, and population movement. Because Khartoum remains central to Sudan's trade and logistics networks, disruptions could affect food and fuel availability beyond the immediate conflict areas. Insecurity in densely populated urban areas would likely drive displacement eastwards or towards neighbouring countries, including Egypt, while discouraging returns. Protection risks would increase, including looting, arbitrary detention, ethnic targeting, abduction, sexual violence, and recruitment or forced conscription of young men and boys by competing factions. Humanitarian access would deteriorate as responders negotiate with multiple armed actors, increasing delays and operational risks. Damage or renewed insecurity around infrastructure and services would further strain health, WASH, shelter, and market systems.

rationale: RSF tactics have increasingly shifted from ground offensives in SAF-controlled areas to long-range drone strikes. The May 2025 strikes on Port Sudan's fuel reservoirs demonstrated RSF's capacity to hit locations far from its main areas of control using long-range kamikaze drones. Port Sudan remains a strategic target because it continues to host key government, technical, and logistical functions, while the Port Sudan-Kassala-Gedaref corridor remains central to Sudan's economy and humanitarian response. Before the conflict, this corridor handled most international trade, and it continues to support imports, fuel supplies, and humanitarian cargo entering SAF-controlled areas. Targeting the corridor would allow RSF to undermine SAF supply chains and disrupt commercial and aid flows without needing to control territory in eastern Sudan. The likelihood of more frequent or damaging attacks would increase if RSF receives sustained external support, expands cross-border supply networks, or gains greater long-range drone capacity. Regional tensions around the Red Sea may further increase the corridor's strategic sensitivity.

text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) resumed long-range drone attacks across areas held by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), increasing the threat to infrastructure supporting eastern supply routes. On 12 August, suspected RSF drones targeted Ad Damar, Al Obeid, Atbara, Bahri, and Um Durman; SAF air defences intercepted several drones, but others struck a mosque and an electricity transformer in Bahri and targets in Al Obeid, killing two people. On 18 August, SAF reported intercepting two RSF FH-95 drones near Jargeira and Bara, while further attacks were reported around Bara, Gebrat Al Sheikh, and the export route towards Al Obeid. The widening geographic reach and repeated attacks indicate an increased likelihood of disruption to transport and supply flows, although Port Sudan itself was not struck..

vulnerability: Port Sudan and the eastern corridor have limited redundancy because alternative routes into SAF-controlled Sudan are constrained, less reliable, or operationally costly. The port is a major entry point for food, fuel, medical supplies, and humanitarian assistance, and disruptions could affect populations far beyond the city. Urban households and IDPs are especially vulnerable because they rely heavily on markets for food and other essentials. Humanitarian operations also depend on fuel, warehouses, roads, and dispatch capacity from Port Sudan to reach other parts of Sudan. Coping capacity is limited by already stretched supply chains, high transport costs, insecurity along inland routes, and dependence on fuel for power generation, water systems, cold chains, and health services. If attacks damage infrastructure or disrupt fuel availability, service providers and responders may have few rapid alternatives.
expected_impact: Repeated drone attacks on Port Sudan or the Port Sudan-Kassala-Gedaref corridor would likely disrupt trade and humanitarian supply flows into SAF-controlled areas. Damage to fuel depots, warehouses, port facilities, roads, or transport hubs could delay imports and onward dispatch, particularly if insecurity persists over several weeks. This would likely contribute to localised shortages and price increases for food, fuel, medicines, and other essential commodities, affecting urban populations, IDPs, and market-dependent households first. Fuel disruptions would have wider knock-on effects: humanitarian transport would slow, operational costs would rise, and the ability to move food, medical supplies, and relief items to field hubs would decline. Reduced fuel and power availability could also undermine WASH systems, water pumping, health facilities, cold chains, and disease response capacity. Although direct physical exposure may be concentrated around the corridor, the humanitarian consequences could extend across central and northern Sudan because of the corridor's central role in national supply chains.

rationale: Since 2025, RSF has expanded its long-range drone capabilities, including kamikaze munitions able to target infrastructure far inside SAF-controlled areas. Northern and River Nile states have already experienced repeated drone attacks on infrastructure, including strikes affecting Merowe Dam and associated power facilities. These attacks have mostly caused temporary disruptions rather than sustained structural damage, but they demonstrate intent and reach. The risk would increase if SAF-RSF fighting intensifies and RSF continues receiving external support that improves its long-range strike capacity. RSF has a clear strategic incentive to target Merowe Dam because it is Sudan's largest hydroelectric dam and supports electricity generation, irrigation, and economic activity across areas under SAF control. Disrupting the dam or the associated electricity grid would allow RSF to increase pressure on SAF governance, undermine public confidence, and disrupt services in areas away from front lines. While imminent large-scale escalation in Northern state is not clearly indicated, the dam's strategic importance makes damaging attacks a credible medium-term risk.

text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as damage to the Merowe power system caused widespread and prolonged electricity disruptions across areas under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces. In early August, a fire at the Merowe Dam power station damaged transmission lines, leaving Khartoum, Northern, Red Sea, and River Nile states without stable electricity for nearly two weeks. Electricity was restored to Khartoum, Red Sea, and River Nile states on 16 August after repairs to damaged cables and a key transformer substation. Repeated drone attacks have also targeted Merowe infrastructure since the start of the conflict. Although the cause of the August fire was not established, the prolonged outage demonstrated the vulnerability of the Merowe-linked power system and its wider impact on essential services..

vulnerability: Northern, central, and eastern Sudan rely heavily on electricity linked to Merowe Dam for public services, health facilities, water pumping, irrigation, and economic activity. Repair capacity, spare parts, and replacement infrastructure are likely constrained by conflict, import limitations, and insecurity. Hospitals, dialysis centres, surgical services, vaccine cold chains, water systems, and displacement sites would have limited coping capacity if blackouts last days or weeks. IDPs in overcrowded shelters and areas with poor water and sanitation are especially vulnerable to disease outbreaks if pumping and treatment systems fail. Farming communities dependent on electric-powered irrigation also have limited alternatives, particularly during cultivation periods. Any damage would therefore affect both immediate service delivery and livelihoods, with consequences extending beyond Northern state to Khartoum, Port Sudan, and other dependent urban centres.
expected_impact: Damage to Merowe Dam or associated grid infrastructure would likely cause widespread power outages across northern, central, and eastern Sudan, including Khartoum, Port Sudan, Ad Dabbah, Atbara, Dongola, and other dependent areas. Depending on repair capacity and the scale of damage, outages could persist for days or weeks. Health facilities would struggle to maintain surgeries, dialysis, oxygen services, vaccine preservation, and emergency care. WASH systems and water pumping would be disrupted, increasing waterborne disease risks, especially in overcrowded IDP sites and areas already facing poor sanitation. Power loss would also affect cold chains, communication, public services, and humanitarian operations. Irrigated agriculture linked to schemes such as Al Hamdab, Al Manasir, Amri, and Kihaila could be disrupted, reducing yields, household income, and food availability. Damage during cultivation periods would worsen livelihood losses and food insecurity, while repeated attacks could reduce confidence in relatively stable northern areas and undermine coping capacity over time.
