rationale: Deteriorating humanitarian conditions, aid shortfalls, and insecurity in eastern Chad are increasingly pushing Sudanese refugees to return to unsafe areas in Darfur, particularly West Darfur. Return movements rose in early 2026, with April arrivals into West Darfur nearly doubling compared with November 2025 levels. Many returnees cited access to resources, services, and humanitarian assistance as a main driver, suggesting that deteriorating conditions in displacement are influencing return decisions. Funding cuts and reduced assistance in Chad have weakened refugee coping capacity and strained already overstretched refugee-hosting areas. Planned relocations away from the Sudan border, following RSF cross-border attacks and Chadian military deployment, may increase uncertainty and pressure on some households to return prematurely. Political instability and tensions within Chad, including dynamics linked to alleged external support for RSF and tensions among groups affected by violence in Darfur, could make refugee-hosting areas less predictable. These factors may increase unsafe returns to Darfur despite continuing insecurity, limited services, and protection risks.

text: The risk remained stable in July 2026, with continued pressure on Sudanese refugees and returnees in Chad, although there was no clear evidence of a sudden mass return movement into West Darfur during the month. By 30 June, more than 1.33 million people had crossed into Chad since the start of the Sudan crisis, including over 405,000 Chadian returnees, with further arrivals expected as conflict and food insecurity persist in Darfur. At the same time, severe funding shortfalls continued to reduce access to food, water, shelter, protection, and healthcare for refugees in Chad, weakening coping capacities in refugee-hosting areas.

vulnerability: West Darfur is poorly positioned to absorb large return movements. Health and WASH services remain limited, with weak vaccination and supplementation coverage, restricted water access, and poor sanitation. Economic conditions are fragile, with inflation, high fuel costs, bank closures, and limited purchasing power constraining food access. IPC projections indicate significant acute food insecurity, while displacement sites and urban areas are already overcrowded and under-served. Returnees may arrive with few assets and face destroyed infrastructure, damaged roads, limited livelihood opportunities, and homes that are occupied, damaged, or destroyed. Protection risks are severe in RSF-dominated areas, especially for non-Arab communities such as Masalit and Zaghawa, who may face intimidation, movement restrictions, looting, ethnically motivated violence, detention, and property-related tensions during transit and upon return.
expected_impact: Increased return movements from Chad would add pressure to West Darfur's already strained services, markets, shelters, and displacement sites. Returnees would likely require shelter, food, protection, health, WASH, and livelihood support, while host communities would face additional pressure on limited water, sanitation, health services, land, and markets. Overcrowding and poor WASH conditions would increase disease outbreak risks, particularly where vaccination and supplementation coverage are weak. Food insecurity would worsen as returnees and host households face high prices, limited income opportunities, and disrupted markets. Protection impacts would be significant: returnees may face movement restrictions, looting, intimidation, arbitrary detention, sexual violence, ethnically motivated attacks, and disputes over housing, land, and property. Non-Arab returnees may be particularly exposed when travelling through or returning to RSF-controlled areas. Damage to homes, roads, markets, and services would slow reintegration and could trigger secondary displacement if households cannot safely resettle or access livelihoods.

R1058.title: El Niño-driven agricultural losses and water shortages in the Philippines increase food security, WASH, and health needs

triggers.title: Below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures
triggers.description: El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation. Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers. Sources: ([PAGASA Accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/el-nino-la-nina/monitoring); [PIA 05/06/2026](https://pia.gov.ph/news/el-nino-to-emerge-in-june-intensify-into-strong-to-very-strong-condition-by-year-end-pagasa/); [FAO accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.fao.org/in-action/drought-portal/preparedness/vulnerability-and-impact-assessment/national-case-studies/the-philippines-case/en)) Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 08-07-2026 Last update: 08-07-2026

rationale: The Philippines faces an increasing risk of El Niño-driven drought, potentially triggering water shortages, agricultural losses, and heat stress in the coming months. El Niño conditions are already present in the tropical Pacific, with sea surface temperature anomalies reaching the +0.5° C threshold in May 2026; most models indicate an over 80% probability of full development, persisting until early 2027 at strong to very strong intensity.

Seasonal forecasts anticipate below-average precipitation across central and southern regions from July–September, extending nationwide from October. The provinces likely to be affected are Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Kalinga, La Union, Mountain Province, Nueva Ecija, Nueva Vizcaya, Pangasinan, Quirino, and Tarlac. Temperatures are forecast above seasonal averages nationwide from July–December. This is likely to produce a poor monsoon season (May–October), vital for maize and rice production, affecting both rain-fed and irrigated crops. Main season rice, harvested in December, accounts for 60% of domestic production.

The Philippines has experienced 12 major drought events since 1968. It is estimated that agricultural drought caused approximately 20 million metric tons of crop losses between 1980–2020. Between July 2023 and April 2024, El Niño-related dry conditions affected multiple provinces, causing agricultural losses, water shortages, and livelihood disruptions. The Department of Social Welfare and Development reported thousands of farming households affected by prolonged dry spells, with losses in some provinces reaching hundreds of millions of pesos. This event also drove extreme heat, school disruptions, and mounting pressure on water and food systems – illustrating how El Niño can rapidly become a multisector humanitarian crisis for affected communities.

In the next one to three months, primary concerns include localised rainfall deficits, water stress, and heat-related impacts, particularly in affected agricultural zones. Over the next three to six months, if El Niño strengthens as projected, drought conditions could intensify significantly, leading to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, water shortages, rising food prices, and worsening livelihood pressures. This may increase humanitarian needs in the WASH, food security, and health sectors, particularly in already-vulnerable rural communities.

text: The risk has increased as El Niño strengthens, with impacts on agriculture and water availability already reported in parts of the Philippines. A strong to very strong El Niño is expected to persist through the first half of 2027 and may peak before the end of 2026. In Davao region, 4,447 farmers have been affected, with approximately 4,791 hectares of crops damaged and PHP 444 million in losses since El Niño emerged in August. Rice production has been particularly affected. In Agusan del Sur province, low river levels, cracked rice fields, dry-spell damage to corn plantations, and critically low water supplies at the provincial government centre were reported in September. Further intensification could increase crop losses and water shortages, reducing agricultural income and access to water among farming communities. These impacts could increase food security and WASH needs over the coming months. The nationwide scale of humanitarian needs remains unclear.

vulnerability: The Philippines is highly exposed to El Niño impacts because agriculture, hydropower, water supply, and rural livelihoods are sensitive to rainfall variability. Rain-fed farming systems, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces, are especially exposed to rainfall deficits and prolonged dry spells. Smallholder farmers, low-income households, and communities reliant on shallow groundwater or seasonal water sources face heightened vulnerability owing to limited adaptive capacity and reduced financial resilience.

The country is also entering the forecast El Niño period with reduced resilience from recent shocks. In 2025, several typhoons caused significant agricultural damage and crop losses, including Typhoon-turned-Super Typhoon Fung-wong (Uwan) and Typhoon Kalmaegi (Tino), which disrupted livelihoods and weakened recovery capacity in affected farming communities. The June 2026 Sarangani earthquake also caused widespread infrastructure damage, displacement, and disruptions to essential services in parts of Mindanao, further straining local response capacity.

Vulnerability is particularly high in Mindanao, where drought risk intersects with multiple compounding shocks, including conflict, displacement, poverty, and food insecurity. Conflict-affected areas, especially in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, already face constrained access to markets, agricultural land, and basic services, reducing household resilience to climate shocks. These overlapping vulnerabilities may amplify the humanitarian impact of drought, as affected communities may have fewer coping options and reduced capacity to absorb livelihood losses.

National coping capacity is supported by strong early warning and disaster management systems, including climate monitoring by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council preparedness mechanisms, and local government contingency planning. Prolonged drought, however, may still overwhelm local response capacities, especially in resource-constrained rural areas. The risk may be further compounded by external economic shocks, including potential disruptions to global oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz.
expected_impact: Below-normal rainfall and above-average temperatures are likely to reduce soil moisture, lower reservoir levels, and disrupt irrigation systems, particularly in drought-prone agricultural areas. This may lead to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, and lower household income among farming communities, increasing food insecurity and coping strategies with potentially harmful consequences. Water shortages may affect both domestic consumption and agricultural production, increasing demand for water rationing or emergency water supply interventions.

Heat-related health risks, including dehydration and heat stress, may also increase, particularly among older people, children, outdoor workers, and communities with limited access to cooling or clean water. Indirect economic effects may further worsen humanitarian conditions. If disruptions to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz trigger higher global fuel prices, transport and agricultural production costs may rise significantly. This could contribute to higher food prices, reduced market access, and higher costs for essential goods, compounding El Niño-related livelihood pressures. Combined climate and economic shocks could disproportionately affect poor and rural households with limited coping capacity.

rationale: After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures.

This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025.

This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against communities, including curfews and checkpoints. Ahead of the anticipated offensive, NSAGs are expected to intensify operations to consolidate territorial control, while retaliatory actions during the crackdown could further increase civilian harm. In response, the elected President has proposed Plan Colombia 2.0, aimed at recovering NSAG-controlled territory, eradicating coca cultivation and illegal mining (the primary financing sources for armed groups), and securing record investment in state armed forces, with the political and financial support of the US Government.

As a result, July, the month preceding the new Government's inauguration, is expected to see an intensification of NSAG violence as armed groups seek to consolidate territorial control and prepare ahead of the anticipated military offensive. Over the first 90-day period (August–October), a marked increase in armed clashes with state forces is expected, a trend that should persist throughout the remainder of 2026. These dynamics will directly affect civilian populations in the departments highlighted, where most rural and Indigenous communities reside.

Planned government reforms, including major cuts to state bureaucracy and measures targeting officials linked to the previous administration, could also increase political tensions and trigger social mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the risk.

A historic ‘Super El Niño’ event, forecast to intensify through late 2026, is expected to compound these dynamics. Authorities are warning of extreme heat, drought, and water shortages, with national implications for food security. This adds further pressure on communities in the departments covered by this risk, where access to food is already constrained by confinement and mobility restrictions linked to armed group activity.

text: In September, intensified state operations and continued armed group activity sustained conflict-related protection risks in Colombia. Between January–August, 23,931 people were affected by mass displacement and 80,369 by confinement, with Cauca, Chocó, Norte de Santander, and Putumayo among the most affected departments. In August alone, 5,976 people were displaced and 6,201 confined. The Government’s shift towards military pressure has increased the lethality of operations against armed groups, while attacks using explosive drones remain a concern, particularly in Cauca and Norte de Santander. Further military pressure may redirect armed group activity towards state forces in the short term, while territorial competition, retaliatory attacks, and incursions into contested areas could sustain violence over the following months. Civilians in rural and Indigenous communities remain exposed to displacement, confinement, movement restrictions, and disrupted access to markets and livelihoods.

vulnerability: Colombia is experiencing prolonged and sustained impacts from armed violence, particularly across the departments highlighted in this risk analysis. Chocó, for example, recorded more than 23,000 people confined in 2025 alone, establishing it as the most acutely affected department for this protection concern. Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, Norte de Santander, and Valle del Cauca also hosted the highest numbers of displaced people in 2025, accounting for approximately 60% of the national total. In many of these areas, NSAG presence and social control measures, including checkpoints, curfews, and mobility restrictions, further limit communities’ ability to access livelihoods and essential services. This has placed significant strain on the response capacity of both the State and humanitarian responders, at the same time that populations affected by armed violence require sustained access to food, health, and protection services. Any escalation in clashes linked to the anticipated security offensive risks further increasing humanitarian needs and constraining operational access.
expected_impact: The expected impact of intensifying NSAG activity and a state military offensive extends to the entire population of the departments highlighted, approximately 10.6 million people, who face risks of forced displacement, confinement, and attacks against civilians. Military operations and armed group retaliation are also expected to increase risks of civilian casualties, attacks against communities, and humanitarian access restrictions in affected areas. Illegal armed group membership has nationally grown by an estimated 23% over the past two years, reaching approximately 27,000 fighters by early 2026 – meaning any return to more active confrontation is likely to be more widespread than in recent cycles of violence.

As an illustrative precedent, the January 2025 escalation between the National Liberation Army (ELN) and dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia in Catatumbo (Norte de Santander) – one of the six departments covered by this risk – displaced an estimated 50,000–56,500 people within weeks of the breakdown of peace talks, underscoring how quickly displacement can scale once dialogue ends and active confrontation begins. This is included as 2025 historical baseline context rather than current reporting.

Armed groups in the region have intensified the recruitment of children, including through social media and by targeting rural boarding schools, while threatening teachers and relatives who report such cases. Nationally, child recruitment cases rose sharply through 2025. An intensification of these practices may be anticipated as groups seek to replenish ranks ahead of renewed confrontation.

Confinement – which already prevented over 137,000 people across the country from leaving their communities between January–August 2025, a significant increase from 2024 – is expected to further increase, restricting affected populations’ access to food, healthcare, and other essential goods and services. These impacts may be compounded by forecasted climate pressures, including drought and water shortages linked to the ‘Super El Niño’, which could further worsen food insecurity in communities already affected by conflict-related mobility restrictions.

Among the highlighted population, cross-border migrants and refugees living along the Venezuelan border who work in Colombia and periodically return home represent a high-risk group, as escalating conflict would hinder their international movement and their ability to afford food and housing. Farmers and Indigenous communities in the rural areas with the strongest NSAG presence are similarly disproportionately exposed.

rationale: There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.

Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. With far-right coalition partners Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism continuing to advocate expanding Israeli control over Gaza and negotiations on a durable ceasefire and post-conflict governance remaining stalled, the Likud-led caretaker government, in place since the Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, will very probably prioritise maintaining operational momentum in Gaza while avoiding the political and military risks associated with a large-scale offensive.

Territorial expansion is expected to continue through a combination of military and engineering measures that progressively transform temporary military positions into more permanent areas of control. Israeli forces are likely to continue advancing the Yellow Line through localised incursions supported by repeated evacuation orders, the demolition of buildings and agricultural land, and the construction of additional military infrastructure, including outposts, surveillance positions, access roads, trenches, and earthen barriers. Recent satellite imagery indicates that Israel has already constructed more than 23km of earth berms and trenches along parts of the Yellow Line, creating a fortified corridor that extends across central Gaza and, in some locations, beyond the original ceasefire demarcation. These measures are likely to be accompanied by the continued expansion of military exclusion zones and restrictions on civilian movement, allowing Israeli forces to consolidate control without undertaking a single large-scale offensive.

text: The risk has deteriorated during August 2026 ahead of the 27 October Israeli elections, as Israeli military control continues to consolidate across Gaza. Further westward advancement of the Yellow Line into eastern Middle Area, Gaza city, and Khan Younis, alongside Israel’s approval of the Green Rafah infrastructure project in eastern Rafah under military supervision, indicates that temporary military positions are increasingly becoming permanent areas of control. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of the US-backed 15-point road map on 8 August, with Jared Kushner subsequently confirming that implementation was contingent on full Hamas disarmament, has reduced prospects for diplomatic measures that could constrain this consolidation before the elections. The expansion is already affecting humanitarian operations, with Yellow Line advances triggering evacuation and shelter-in-place orders affecting more than ten UNRWA premises, indicating that further territorial consolidation is likely to compound existing access constraints and accelerate the deterioration of humanitarian operational capacity..

vulnerability: People in Gaza already had very high humanitarian needs before the increased Israeli bombardment that has persisted since October 2023. Nearly three years of conflict have left the entire population (2.1 million people) in need of assistance, with 76.6% of housing units (371,888 out of 485,361) destroyed or damaged and more than 50% of hospitals non-functional. Nearly 90% of water and sanitation infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged, and no hospital is fully functional, while 39% (14/36) of hospitals remain partially functional. More than 1.9 million people (90% of the population) have been displaced, often multiple times, and are living in overcrowded, unsafe, or makeshift conditions, needing continued emergency shelter and essential NFIs. 63% of assessed households access less than the minimum 6L emergency standard of water per day. Amid continued shortages in medical supplies, acute watery diarrhoea remains among the most reported illnesses, though recent weekly trends have fluctuated; cases were reported to be decreasing by late June 2026 after earlier seasonal summer spikes. Coping capacity is minimal and almost entirely aid-dependent, with 83% of households reporting no income, and only 3% of cropland is usable, so the gains recorded since the ceasefire rest entirely on humanitarian assistance.
expected_impact: If this risk materialises, humanitarian conditions will deteriorate most acutely in areas adjacent to the expanding Yellow Line, particularly eastern Gaza city (including At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya), the Netzarim corridor in central Gaza, eastern Deir Al Balah, and northern Khan Younis. These areas may be the most affected because they lie along the current trajectory of Israeli territorial expansion and have experienced repeated military operations, evacuation orders, and engineering activities since late June 2026. Continued territorial consolidation would further reduce the already-limited areas available for civilians, increasing overcrowding in displacement sites and placing additional pressure on humanitarian service delivery.

Additional displacement would increase shelter needs at a time when humanitarian capacity is declining; the number of families receiving shelter assistance fell by 37% between May–June 2026 because of funding shortages and access restrictions.

Humanitarian access is highly likely to become increasingly constrained as the expanding Yellow Line reduces humanitarian operational space and fragments access routes. Additional military exclusion zones, fortifications, and engineering works will require more frequent coordination with Israeli authorities, limit access to communities near the evolving front line, and force humanitarian responders to rely on fewer approved corridors. This is expected to delay aid deliveries, hinder needs assessments, and limit infrastructure repairs.

Food security and livelihoods will probably deteriorate further from already critical levels. Between April–June 2026, 59% of Gaza's population faced Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food insecurity, including around 212,000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) conditions. Further expansion of the Yellow Line would reduce access to agricultural land and remaining livelihood opportunities while restricting humanitarian food deliveries and market access. This would increase reliance on aid and deepen acute food insecurity.

Health and WASH conditions are likely to worsen from an already-overstretched baseline. Health facilities continue to face severe supply shortages, while 63% of assessed households receive less than 6L of water per person per day. The expansion of the Yellow Line would further restrict humanitarian access for medical referrals, infrastructure repairs, and supply deliveries, increasing pressure on health services and the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks and preventable deaths.

rationale: Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes.

The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After launching Operation Ghazab lil Haq on 21 February, Pakistani authorities declared open war against Afghanistan's Interim Taliban Authority. Despite a two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April negotiated by China, these attacks have continued, forming a pattern of ‘coercive diplomacy’ between the two countries. This coercive diplomacy has seen fighting continue until it becomes less productive for either side, at which point they briefly return to negotiations until a new security incident restarts the cycle. This pattern is expected to persist in waves over the next three to six months rather than resolve into a stable ceasefire.

The current tension heightens protection risks for civilians in border-adjacent Afghan provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika), including casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, as well as exposure to explosive remnants of war and unexploded ordnance in areas affected by shelling.

Displacement towards other regions of Afghanistan is expected to persist over the next three to six months. The closure of and restricted movement at the Torkham, Chaman, and other crossings along the Durand Line, whether from active conflict or checkpoint closures, could trap civilians in insecure areas or block access to services on the other side. Host communities already sheltering IDPs and returnees face added strain, raising the risk of tension and disputes over limited resources and services.

The closure of border crossings has also halted transit flows and delayed humanitarian and commercial supplies. Afghanistan is highly dependent on food imports, as domestic production cannot meet national demand. This dependence, combined with the depletion of harvest stocks in September and declining agricultural labour opportunities from the seasonal downturn in October, is likely to worsen food insecurity. As a result, market dependence is expected to increase, reducing household income and heightening the risk of food consumption gaps.

text: Protection risks for communities in border areas increased in September as clashes and cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan resumed after a temporary decline. Repeated Pakistani airstrikes and Afghan military operations have heightened the risk of civilian casualties, damage to homes, and displacement, particularly in eastern Afghanistan. Pakistan said its strikes on 21 September killed 28 fighters, while Afghan officials reported civilian casualties; the UN confirmed three civilian deaths. On 27 September, Afghan forces reported killing 28 fighters and capturing 32 in Nuristan province after they crossed from Pakistan. Further Pakistani strikes on 1 October targeted locations in Afghanistan, including Kunar and Helmand provinces. Pakistan reported 22 militants killed and weapons depots destroyed, while Taliban authorities reported 9–10 civilian deaths, including women and children, and damage to homes. The conflicting accounts highlight the risks to civilians in affected areas, where renewed hostilities could cause further casualties, displacement, and disrupted access to essential services.

vulnerability: People have little coping capacity as Afghanistan is experiencing a weak economy, is subject to international sanctions, and has suffered major cuts in international aid, including a complete halt in USAID support. At the beginning of 2026, an estimated 17.5 million people needed humanitarian aid; up until 2025, 85% of the population lived below the poverty line of USD 1 a day.

People in border areas are experiencing the consequences of clashes and tensions between the two governments. Between January–March 2026, cross-border attacks by Pakistani forces killed and injured over 750 Afghan civilians, most from air strikes in eastern and southern Afghanistan.

Afghanistan–Pakistan transit trade has suffered one of its steepest declines, plunging to just 11,592 containers worth USD 367 million in the outgoing fiscal year from nearly 89,000 containers valued at USD 5 billion before the Taliban returned to power, as Kabul’s growing reliance on Iranian routes and Pakistan’s border curbs reshaped the decades-old trade corridor. Continued conflict and border closures are likely to further restrict trade and humanitarian supply flows over the next three to six months, compounding food insecurity in affected provinces.

Communities in bordering areas are dealing with a scarcity of food and essential services. People are often forced to implement potentially harmful coping mechanisms, such as child marriage in exchange for food and money.

Pakistan continues to serve as Afghanistan's primary overland transit route for international humanitarian assistance, and the conflict escalation further restricts access for humanitarian aid. Only until 13 July, Pakistani customs authorities issued gate passes for 26 containers carrying food and essential relief supplies after completing customs formalities. The latest clearance does not signal a reopening of the crossing but provides a limited humanitarian exemption to facilitate UN relief operations.
expected_impact: Populations along the Durand Line will experience high protection risks. Civilian casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, particularly in border-adjacent provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, and Paktika), will likely occur. There is also a high risk of damage to civilian infrastructure, homes, markets, and health facilities, reducing safe access to essential services.

An estimated 21.9 million people are in need across Afghanistan in 2026, including 15 million in need of protection and 4.2 million in need of shelter and site management support. This figure may not account for the estimated 500,000 conflict-displaced people.

The conflict is likely to impede access to services, deteriorate the livelihoods of people, particularly returnees recently reported from Pakistan and Iran. There were over 2.5 million returnees from Iran and Pakistan in 2025, adding pressure on overstretched local resources, services, and livelihoods.

Forced displacement is expected to persist and is likely to increase, causing a deterioration of humanitarian needs in provinces along the Durand Line. In April 2026 alone, over 9,000 families were forced to leave their homes given the rocket attacks conducted by Pakistani forces on areas near the Durand Line in Afghanistan’s Kunar province.

The provinces of Kunar, Laghman, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika are projected to remain in Stressed (IPC Phase 2) food security conditions or deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) during the lean season. Paktika has been among the most affected provinces, experiencing repeated cross-border shelling that has damaged civilian infrastructure and displaced communities, reducing access to health services and agricultural livelihoods. The situation is partly caused by the prolonged closure of key Durand Line crossings, impeding the trade and import of food and directly affecting food security and livelihoods in Afghanistan. Growing uncertainty around commodity movements through Iran because of the volatile Middle East conflict is also driving up logistics costs and reducing the availability of essential goods in local markets. Further conflict escalation along the Durand Line is likely to  delay any reopening of border crossings and halt the limited humanitarian convoys currently permitted through, further reducing the availability of essential goods and deepening food insecurity.

The direct impact of conflict escalation on civilian protection and humanitarian access is expected to be the primary driver of increased need. Casualties, displacement, and restricted humanitarian access caused by persistent air strikes and border closures are likely to push additional populations into IPC 3 before food insecurity peaks. Up to 2.3 million additional people could become food-insecure as a result of a prolonged border closure with Pakistan and further conflict escalation. At the same time, food assistance currently reaches only 2.7% of the population because of governmental restrictions and funding shortfalls.

By October 2026, the depletion of household harvest stocks and the seasonal decline in agricultural labour will increase market dependence just as conflict-driven border closures at Torkham are expected to drive prices upwards through the lean season peak from December–January. The situation is compounded by high unemployment and declining remittance inflows.

rationale: On 13 July 2026, the Iran-backed de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) announced the end of a de facto period of de-escalation with Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen, increasing the risk of renewed cross-border and intra-Yemeni hostilities following a series of retaliatory actions. On the same day, the IRG said it had struck Sana'a International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, while the DFA accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the attack. The DFA subsequently retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks against Abha International Airport, marking the first attack on Saudi territory since the 2022 truce. On 20 July, the DFA announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, describing it as a response to Saudi restrictions on DFA-controlled airports and seaports. The DFA has already targeted several vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, in an attempt to enforce the blockade.

Fighting has also intensified between the DFA and the IRG along front lines in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta’iz, predating but compounded by the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations. Saudi Arabia is the main IRG backer, and the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations has already prompted expanded military involvement. From 24–25 July, the Saudi-led coalition conducted strikes in Al Hodeidah, while the IRG air force struck DFA missile and drone launch sites and weapons facilities in Ma'rib and Al Jawf. These developments indicate that the escalation has expanded beyond isolated cross-border retaliation, increasing the risk of sustained intra-Yemeni conflict.

The first cross-border attack on Saudi Arabia since the truce is significant because it signals that both parties are becoming increasingly willing to use direct military force to pursue their objectives, weakening one of the key restraints that has sustained the de facto ceasefire. Both Saudi Arabia and the DFA have incentives to avoid a renewed large-scale conflict. Saudi Arabia seeks to protect its economic interests and avoid another costly war, while the DFA is unlikely to escalate unless it perceives increased Saudi military involvement or an opportunity to improve its strategic position. A miscalculation could trigger the renewal of conflict. Further attacks on Saudi territory or attempts to enforce a blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait would increase the likelihood of expanded or sustained Saudi and international military involvement in the Red Sea and Yemen. Saudi Arabia has already announced plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition on 30 July 2026.

Escalations between the DFA and Saudi Arabia would likely intensify fighting between the DFA and the Saudi-backed IRG, further restricting humanitarian access. Saudi air strikes on seaports and airports would disrupt commercial and humanitarian imports, triggering new displacement. Supply chain disruptions would increase commodity prices and erode purchasing power. Any disruption to shipping through the Bab Al Mandab Strait would also have cascading impacts on regional and global supply chains while aggravating needs in a country where over 22 million people require humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure.
vulnerability: Yemen continues to face one of the world's largest humanitarian crises, with 22.3 million people requiring assistance, including 5.2 million IDPs. Food insecurity remains the most critical need; over 5.4 million people are projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse conditions between June–September 2026. Of these, 1.6 million are experiencing Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity. Health and WASH systems remain severely overstretched; only 59.3% of health facilities are fully functional, and 14.4 million people require WASH assistance, with the highest-severity needs concentrated in Abyan, Ad Dali', Al Bayda, Al Hodeidah, Dhamar, Hajjah, Lahj, Ma’rib, Raymah, and Ta’iz. Continued conflict, localised insecurity, displacement, economic decline, disease outbreaks, and climate shocks have eroded livelihoods and coping capacities, leaving communities highly vulnerable to renewed hostilities, explosive ordnance, protection risks, disruptions to essential services and humanitarian assistance, and further displacement

In IRG-controlled areas. Humanitarian food assistance currently supports 1.7 million people, preventing more severe food insecurity, but funding shortfalls are expected to reduce assistance to 1.2 million people receiving only one-third of typical rations during the 2026 lean season. Seasonal agricultural production and religious transfers (zakat and sadaqah) provide only temporary relief, while irregular salaries, high food prices, and deteriorating livelihoods continue to undermine resilience.
expected_impact: Renewed cross-border hostilities and intensified frontline fighting would likely increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian needs, particularly in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta'iz. Escalating insecurity would further restrict humanitarian access, delay needs assessments, and disrupt the delivery of food, health, WASH, and protection assistance, especially in frontline communities and those with specific access constraints.

Saudi air strikes on transport infrastructure, seaports, and fuel supply routes, together with increased insecurity around the Bab Al Mandab Strait, would likely disrupt commercial imports and humanitarian supply chains. Higher shipping insurance premiums, transport costs, and fuel shortages would increase food and commodity prices, further reducing household purchasing power in a country heavily dependent on imports. Fuel shortages would also disrupt electricity generation, water pumping, health services, and the cold chain for medicines and vaccines, increasing the risk of disease outbreaks.

Escalation would likely trigger new displacement while exposing civilians to explosive ordnance and other protection risks. Households already experiencing severe food insecurity would have fewer coping options as livelihoods, markets, and humanitarian assistance are disrupted.

rationale: Violence involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) is rising after five years of declining lethality in the Lake Chad Basin. More than 300 clashes involving the two groups were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, 30% above the previous quarter, while militant Islamist-linked fatalities increased by 28% over the past year, reaching their highest level since 2015. Nigeria accounted for 87% of these fatalities, with Borno remaining the expected epicentre, followed by affected areas of Adamawa and Yobe.

The escalation is expected to be driven by two related developments. While regional forces have concentrated military operations against ISWAP, Boko Haram has regrouped and rebuilt its capacity to launch coordinated attacks against military bases. At the same time, the May killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal Al Minuki is expected to trigger retaliatory attacks and greater competition between factions for territorial influence and legitimacy. ISWAP has overrun at least 16 Nigerian military bases over the past year, while its increasing use of improvised explosive devices and reconnaissance drones enhances its capacity to identify, isolate, and attack military positions, increasing the operational threat posed by the group.

Over the next three to six months, there is a very high probability that intensified insurgent attacks and military counteroperations will increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints across the basin. Violence is expected to remain concentrated in Borno, with continued spillover into Adamawa and Yobe, where Boko Haram and ISWAP are likely to intensify attacks on civilians, military positions, and transport routes. Escalating violence in northeastern Nigeria is expected to generate additional refugee movements into Niger's Diffa region, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may contribute to increased attacks, abductions, and disruptions to fishing and trade in Cameroon’s Far North, as well as renewed displacement and protection risks in Chad’s Lac province. These cross-border displacement dynamics and parallel insecurity are expected to reverse recent stabilisation gains and generate additional humanitarian needs across the Lake Chad Basin.

text: The risk continued to increase in the second half of September, with persistent armed group activity generating new displacement and protection concerns in Cameroon's Far North region. On 17 September, armed assailants killed at least 15 civilians in Madegoua, near Makary commune in Logone et Chari division. While no group claimed responsibility, a security analyst assessed that Islamic State West Africa Province was likely responsible. The attack prompted several hundred people from around ten nearby villages to flee towards Kousseri, Mora, and Waza, where new arrivals faced inadequate food and shelter and increased pressure on local health services. Insecurity remained persistent elsewhere in Far North region during September, including attempted attacks by Islamic State West Africa Province on security positions near Fotokol and continued Boko Haram abductions. These developments reinforce the risk of further displacement and protection needs in border communities and demonstrate that sustained armed group activity is translating into humanitarian impacts despite continued military operations.

vulnerability: The Lake Chad Basin already faces severe humanitarian vulnerabilities after more than a decade of conflict, displacement, and chronic underdevelopment. Across Cameroon, Chad, Niger, and Nigeria, more than 3.5 million people are forcibly displaced, and 8.2 million require humanitarian assistance. Recurrent violence, weak state presence in remote border areas, and limited access to basic services have reduced communities’ ability to cope with additional shocks. Protection risks remain particularly acute for women, children, displaced populations, and communities living in isolated border and island areas.

Many households depend on fishing, livestock herding, cross-border trade, and small-scale agriculture for their livelihoods. Repeated attacks, extortion, movement restrictions, and insecurity along transport routes have disrupted these activities, reducing incomes and increasing food insecurity. In several areas, communities face limited access to education, healthcare, and protection services, while repeated displacement has eroded traditional support networks and coping mechanisms.

Humanitarian responders maintain a significant presence across the basin, but insecurity, logistical constraints, underfunding, and access restrictions continue to limit the scale and reach of assistance. A continued deterioration of security conditions would further strain already-overstretched services, reduce humanitarian access, and weaken the coping capacity of conflict-affected communities and host populations.
expected_impact: Borno state is expected to remain the epicentre of the crisis, with intensified attacks by ISWAP and Boko Haram likely to generate additional displacement, civilian casualties, and humanitarian access restrictions. Spillover into Adamawa and Yobe may further disrupt transport corridors, markets, and access to health and education services in affected communities. In Niger’s Diffa region, the main humanitarian impact is expected to result from additional refugee arrivals fleeing violence in northeastern Nigeria, increasing pressure on host communities, protection services, and humanitarian assistance. In Cameroon’s Far North, renewed attacks, abductions, and restrictions on fishing and cross-border trade may further erode livelihoods and increase protection risks in border communities. In Chad’s Lac province, renewed attacks and military operations may trigger secondary displacement, restrict civilian movement, and increase pressure on already-overstretched basic services. Across the basin, increased insecurity is expected to further constrain humanitarian access, particularly along transport routes and in remote border and island communities. Additional displacement and livelihood disruptions are likely to increase humanitarian needs and place further pressure on civic authorities and humanitarian responders across the four countries.

rationale: Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities.

Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting.

ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. This indicates Badakhshan province is becoming a potential point for national conflict risk.

The province has valuable mineral deposits, including gold and lapis lazuli, and has long been contested. Recent clashes were triggered by the ITA suspension of gold mining activities in parts of the province to disarm fighters of opposition groups.

Clashes have occurred across multiple districts in 2026, including a brief seizure of the Yaftal-e Sufla district headquarters and Afghanistan Freedom Front clashes with ITA forces in Zebak in July. Repeated fighting over district centres risks triggering intermittent displacement as families flee active front lines and may expose residents to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and casualties. Badakhshan’s current context indicates a risk of rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating food security outlook.

text: Clashes between armed groups and Taliban forces continued in Badakhshan province in September. Between 29 August and 25 September, battles increased by 68% (eight events) and organised violence by 31% (11 events) compared with the previous year’s average. On 30 September, the Afghanistan Freedom Front reported Taliban attacks in Zebak district, following repeated clashes in recent weeks. On 29 September, the Taliban Defence Ministry declared its operation over in Kamdesh district, Nuristan province, claiming 41 people killed and 62 detained. Continued fighting could expose rural communities to casualties, movement restrictions, forced recruitment, and disruptions to education and livelihoods, although these impacts remain unverified. Humanitarian needs are compounded by food insecurity: an estimated 671,800 people (at least 40% of Badakhshan’s population) face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse. Below-average harvests and above-national-average prices for rice, sugar, and cooking oil are likely to further constrain food access. Limited vaccination coverage and access barriers in remote areas also increase vulnerability to measles outbreaks.

vulnerability: The entire Badakhshan province is currently experiencing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity levels according to FEWS NET, but IPC assessments place it in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through the current period.

The wheat harvest is still in its early stages as harvesting begins later at higher elevations. The delay in harvest impedes households’ access to harvest-related food and income and keeps them reliant on market purchases in the meantime. Staple food prices are elevated by the high cost of transport to these remote areas, while household income is further constrained by below-average labour opportunities. Poor households in the province are already reporting food consumption gaps and depleting assets; intensified conflict would likely accelerate this depletion by disrupting markets, movement, and livelihoods, pushing more households towards potentially harmful coping strategies.

Above-average precipitation – in the form of increased snowfall at higher elevations and increased rain and snow at lower elevations, particularly between October–April – is expected, and this is plausibly positive for the harvest, improving water availability after several drought-affected seasons. On the other hand, favourable weather conditions may fail to translate into higher production if farmers are unable to access fertiliser before and during the autumn planting period amid rising prices.

There is limited information about health in the province, although communities have reported shortages of medicines and adequate facilities; there are also reports of substance use in place of unavailable medicines. In July 2026, the Health Cluster reported reaching around 5,300 people in the province. Badakhshan's mountainous terrain also imposes deep access constraints on humanitarian response, meaning any increase in clashes is likely to further restrict access to affected populations.

Recently, the province experienced floods in Shughnan and Maimai districts. Floods damaged schools, 42,800 hectares of cultivated agricultural land, and other critical infrastructure, including bridges and water mills, as well as killing livestock. Flash floods may have displaced explosive ordnance or exposed previous landmines.
expected_impact: Intensified conflict would directly affect communities' protection, with people likely exposed to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and the risk of casualties. Repeated fighting over district centres could trigger short- and medium-term displacement as families flee active front lines, restricting mobility and disrupting livelihoods in turn.

Gold mining disputes between armed groups have disrupted local livelihoods. The ITA has suspended mining in contested areas to cut off income for opposition armed groups, in the process also stripping income from mining-dependent communities, which are not necessarily tied to armed groups. Badakhshan's mines department head reported around 650–700 mining companies, with thousands of people working manually. Thousands of miners are specifically deployed in areas such as Shiwa. Further escalation could mean lost income for miners caught between Taliban control efforts and dissident commanders. Health access, already limited, would likely deteriorate further; communities have already reported shortages of medicines and adequate facilities, as well as substance use in place of unavailable medicines. Escalating conflict increases the risk of health facilities being damaged, occupied, or forced to suspend services and could disrupt the already-limited supply of medicines to clinics.

This livelihood pressure is set against a difficult seasonal outlook. Above-average precipitation expected between October 2026 and April 2027 could damage the upcoming harvest, further eroding food security just as the lean season approaches. Food prices are already rising, and further disruption to markets, movement, and livelihoods could push households towards potentially harmful coping strategies, such as early marriage and skipping meals.

The current context in Badakhshan points to a compounding risk: rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating health and food security outlook..

rationale: Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida.

Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israel a justification to intervene on behalf of the Druze and expand in southern Syria. The proposed corridor would connect the governorate with the Golan area, including Hader near Mount Hermon and Druze villages along the Syrian Golan. Although the proposal was previously rejected by the Syrian transitional Government, renewed violence or deterioration in As Sweida could bring it back into discussions and provide a pretext for expanding Israeli control or establishing protected access through southern Syria. While Israel framed its military intervention during the July 2025 violence as protecting the Druze, Druze opinion remains divided. One senior spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, has welcomed Israeli involvement, while the other two have consistently rejected foreign interference, and As Sweida's Druze security chief warned it had complicated reconciliation.

A second pathway is the activity of Israeli settlers seeking to establish a permanent presence. The Pioneers of Bashan,  an Israeli settler movement, have repeatedly attempted to cross into southern Syria and establish outposts, including around Hader and Mount Hermon, with their stated ambitions extending across As Sweida, Dar'a, and Quneitra governorates. More than 40 settlers entered the outskirts of Hader in April, while approximately 70–100 attempted to cross through Mount Hermon in July, followed by further attempts in August. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data indicates an upward trend in incursion attempts since April 2026, peaking sharply in July with six recorded events. Although the Israel Defense Forces have so far prevented permanent settlement, repeated attempts could increase pressure on Israeli authorities to eventually formalise such activity.

If either pathway materialises, further Israeli control and presence in southern Syria are likely to restrict civilian movement and access to agricultural land through additional checkpoints, patrols, and military restrictions. An expanded Israeli presence could also prompt resistance from Syrian government forces, as well as communities or armed groups in Quneitra and western Dar'a, increasing the probability of clashes around Israeli positions.

text: The risk increased in September as Israeli ground activity in Quneitra and western Dar'a governorates intensified, while tensions in As Sweida persisted. During 1–7 September, 19 Israeli incursions were recorded in Quneitra (13) and Dar'a (6), including house searches, temporary checkpoints, and detentions. On 13 September, Israeli reservists called for deeper advances into southern Syria, while Israeli forces were already operating from 10 positions inside Syrian territory. On 22 September, Israeli forces shelled Jamlah and Abdeen villages in the Yarmouk Basin, followed by five incursions across Quneitra and western Dar'a within 24 hours on 29 September. In As Sweida, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri's factions continued calling for separation from Syria and blocked more than 13,000 students from reaching examination centres. Israel also called for the demilitarisation of Quneitra, Dar'a, and As Sweida, indicating continued efforts to shape the security environment in southern Syria.

vulnerability: There are already 1.37 million people in need in the three governorates exposed to Israeli expansion in southern Syria, including 872,200 in Dar’a, 384,000 in As Sweida, and 110,500 in Quneitra.

In western Dar’a, Israeli military activity, movement restrictions and explosive ordnance contamination have restricted access to farmland and grazing areas and disrupted agricultural livelihoods. By June 2026, more than 32,000 returnees had been recorded in western Dar’a since December 2024, adding pressure to already-overstretched health, water, and education services. In Quneitra and Dar’a, Israeli forces carried out incursions, shelled farmland, and detained civilians through July 2026, restricting access to land and reducing household income. In As Sweida, 32% of assessed communities in May were facing multiple severe needs, mainly related to livelihoods, health, and protection. Renewed insecurity and armed clashes further disrupt livelihoods and access to essential services.

Coping capacity is weakened by limited livelihood opportunities and gaps in humanitarian assistance. By 24 August, 83% of assessed locations in As Sweida reported challenges to the reintegration of displaced people, while limited employment opportunities and depleted savings are constraining households’ ability to meet basic needs. Humanitarian assistance also faces funding constraints, with WFP suspending assistance for more than 72,000 IDPs across As Sweida, Quneitra, and Rural Damascus since the end of July 2026..
expected_impact: If the risk materialises, As Sweida, Dar’a, and Quneitra governorates are expected to face increased displacement, agricultural and livestock livelihood losses, deteriorating food access, and further disruption to water and essential services.

Further Israeli restrictions on farmland and grazing areas would reduce household income and food production. Between 70–80% of communities in southern Syria are dependent on farming for food, but Quneitra households in the immediate border zone have already reduced crop production because of Israeli military operations, further contributing to deteriorating food insecurity. In Dar’a, further restrictions on agricultural land could reduce household income during a critical period for potato and tomato production, with above-average 2026 harvests already generating limited returns because of weak prices and high input costs. Israeli incursions in July also cut agricultural labourers, herders, and farming households off from farmland and grazing areas during the harvest season, reducing cash income.

Expansion of Israeli positions or clashes around outposts and a protected corridor could trigger new displacement, particularly from communities surrounding Israeli positions. As Sweida is particularly exposed, with around 101,000 people internally displaced there by April 2026, equivalent to 21% of its population, while previous violence has displaced thousands towards Dar’a. Further displacement would increase pressure on host communities and already-strained services in Dar’a and As Sweida.

Further Israeli expansion could disrupt access to water infrastructure and sources in western Dar’a villages, particularly around new military positions or along a protected corridor. In Maariya, Israeli military activity around the site between May–June led to the sabotage of the village well, leaving residents dependent on costly private water supplies. In Abdin, piped water has been unavailable for a second consecutive year, with households paying around SYP 150,000 (USD 11.50) per tanker, while critically low water levels in Abdin Dam are already threatening irrigation in the Yarmuk Basin. Further Israeli expansion around these water sources could compound existing shortages, increase household water costs, and disrupt agricultural production.

Men in areas that may be affected by Israeli incursions could face increased protection risks from detention, interrogation, and movement restrictions. Israeli forces have continued to temporarily detain Syrian men during raids and at checkpoints, with some released after hours of questioning, while others have been transferred to Israeli detention facilities for months without publicly stated grounds. By 17 August, Israeli forces were still detaining at least 47 Syrians after the release of over 140 in July..

rationale: By 28 August 2026, an estimated 700–1,000 military personnel were conducting clearance operations around the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Yebyu township after a late-June order to protect the strategic projects. Since 9 July, fighting, raids, arson, looting, arbitrary arrests, and killings have displaced more than 4,500 people from eight Nabule villages. Renewed fighting near the SEZ from 21–22 August caused further civilian displacement. More than 2,000 people were displaced from ten villages in Thayetchaung township in August.

The concentration of military deployments around the project area, following orders to protect strategic infrastructure and agreements to revive the project, indicates that the operation is intended to secure the SEZ. The SEZ is a long-stalled port and industrial zone planned to include a deep-sea port, coal-fired power plant, oil refinery, and liquefied natural gas facilities. The risk is more immediate because Myanmar and Russia revived the project in 2025, signed a June 2026 power plant agreement, and included the Dawei port, refinery, and power plant in their August Moscow agreements. The timing of these deals and the deployment, alongside clashes with the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) near Wet Chaung, makes control of the project area a current strategic objective rather than a remote development scenario.

Over the next six months, military efforts to secure the SEZ are likely to include attempts to control Highway 8, the main north–south route through Tanintharyi, and the Dawei–Htee Khee road, which connects the project area through Myitta to the Thailand border. These routes are important for moving troops and supplies and would support future port and SEZ operations. Continued resistance activities by the KNLA, National Unity Government-affiliated People’s Defence Forces, and other local resistance groups operating in and around the Dawei SEZ could trigger further military sweeps, preventing safe returns and causing new and repeated displacement. Prolonged separation from homes, farms, and plantations will reduce food production and household income, increasing dependence on markets and host communities and worsening food, shelter, and health needs.

text: The risk increased in September as military operations expanded across Launglon, Long Lone, Thayetchaung, and Yebyu townships and along Highway 8. In late September, troops advanced into Thit Taw Taung in Yebyu and Kyauk Sin in Launglon. Operations in Long Lone between 8–10 September killed four civilians and displaced nearly 5,000 people. In Yebyu, increased troop deployments, checkpoints, and questioning restricted civilians’ access to plantations and workplaces, while reports of civilians being forced to guide troops or act as human shields indicate heightened protection risks. Since late September, flooding and landslides have compounded these impacts by damaging roads and communications. Continued military activity has constrained displacement and evacuation, while blocked roads and limited access to machinery have delayed humanitarian assistance to villages isolated by floodwater and landslides. The combination of conflict and natural hazards is likely to increase displacement, restrict access to livelihoods and essential services, and prolong humanitarian access constraints.

vulnerability: The affected area already hosts a large displaced population. Until 17 August 2026, around 267,600 people remained displaced across Tanintharyi region because of conflict since February 2021. A separate estimate identified more than 40,500 displaced people across Dawei, Launglon, Thayetchaung, and Yebyu townships in July. These figures cannot be combined because they cover different areas and use different methodologies. Both, however, indicate that host communities and local support networks are already under significant pressure.

Displacement has become prolonged in parts of Nabule, including Eikani, Khamaung Chaung, and Wet Chaung village tracts. These displaced people commonly seek safety in neighbouring villages, forests, hills, plantations, monasteries, or Dawei town. Some return when troops leave the area but flee again when military operations or fighting resumes. This makes displacement difficult to track and repeatedly disrupts access to shelter, food stocks, documents, livelihoods, and income.

The monsoon season further increases humanitarian needs. People staying in forests and makeshift shelters face heavy rain, flooding, unsafe water, vector-borne diseases, and limited healthcare access. Poor road conditions also affect the delivery of food and relief supplies. In June, nearly two-thirds of displaced people in Tanintharyi were estimated to receive little or no assistance. Limited funding and reliance on small local response networks reduce the capacity to support further displacement.
expected_impact: Further military operations are likely to cause rapid and repeated displacement from villages around the SEZ and its access routes. Households may separate, with some members remaining to protect homes, plantations, and livestock while others seek safety elsewhere. This could complicate family reunification, displacement tracking, and access to assistance. People travelling through checkpoints or returning to their villages will face increased risks of detention, forced recruitment, and exposure to indirect fire.

Families sheltering in forests, plantations, or incomplete structures will face worsening shelter, water, sanitation, and health conditions, particularly during the remainder of the monsoon season. Limited transport and healthcare access may delay treatment, maternal care, and medical referrals.

Food security and livelihoods will worsen as farmers and plantation workers lose access to land, stored food, tools, livestock, and markets. An estimated 877,000 people in Tanintharyi already require humanitarian assistance in 2026, with needs classified as catastrophic (Severity 5) in Launglon and extreme (Severity 4) in Dawei, Thayetchaung, and Yebyu townships. Road insecurity, checkpoints, fuel scarcity, and controls on transported goods may further raise prices and restrict the delivery of food and relief. Host families will absorb additional costs while also facing disrupted local trade.

If physical implementation of the SEZ resumes, temporary displacement could become prolonged. Security perimeters, land demarcation, housing destruction, and missing documentation may prevent returns or pressure affected households to accept relocation or compensation. As operations around the SEZ overlap with wider military activity across Dawei district, newly displaced people may be scattered across different locations and recorded under separate incidents. This could delay verification of their numbers, locations, and needs, increasing the risk that some displaced communities, particularly those moving repeatedly or staying outside formal sites, may be missed during assessments and receive limited or irregular assistance.

Humanitarian access is likely to remain severely constrained as fighting and military checkpoints restrict roads into the SEZ area and limit the movement of food, medicine, shelter materials, and evacuation support. In July, three Burmese aid volunteers were detained while evacuating residents of Kamauk Chaung and later found killed after being used as human shields. This incident may deter grassroots responders from reaching displaced families. Civilians travelling between villages and displacement locations or returning to collect belongings, harvest crops, or tend to livestock will also face heightened risks of arrest, killing, forced recruitment, and use as human shields.
