rationale: Indonesia's annual forest and peatland fire season has intensified sharply during the 2026 dry season. Nearly 95,000 hectares burnt in July alone, almost doubling the area burnt during the first six months of the year and bringing the January–July total to more than 202,000 hectares. By late August, around 285,000 hectares had burnt, and thousands of hotspots were being detected across Kalimantan and Sumatra. West Kalimantan, including Ketapang and Pontianak, is among the areas most affected, while fires are also concentrated in Central Kalimantan and parts of Sumatra, particularly Jambi, Riau, and South Sumatra.

The risk could deteriorate over the next one to three months as El Niño conditions intensify and prolong hotter, drier weather. Fire risk normally peaks during the late dry season, while peatland fires can burn underground, spread beyond visible fire lines, and remain difficult to extinguish. Agricultural land clearing and fires within company concessions are also contributing to the ignition and spread. More than 9,000 hotspots were recorded in August, exceeding the number recorded in the same month during the severe 2015 fire season.

Haze is already affecting populated areas across Kalimantan and Sumatra, particularly Jambi city, Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan, Pekanbaru in Riau, and Pontianak and Singkawang in West Kalimantan, where poor air quality and reduced visibility have disrupted education and transport.

Indonesia has substantial national response capacity. The National Agency for Disaster Countermeasure, provincial authorities, the military, police, and forestry services are conducting ground suppression, water bombing, cloud seeding, hotspot surveillance, and law enforcement operations. By the end of August, authorities had mobilised around 48,000 officers, more than 1,400 volunteers, and 34 firefighting aircraft, while permits had been issued for foreign aircraft. Even so, persistent peat fires, limited water, poor visibility, and simultaneous fires across remote areas could exceed local response capacity and prolong exposure to hazardous smoke. Humanitarian organisations may be required to provide targeted health, education, and livelihood support if the haze persists or national capacity becomes overstretched..

text: The risk increased during September, with haze continuing to disrupt education and transport despite a decline in fire activity. By 9 September, more than 250,000 pupils across 1,030 schools in Palembang, South Sumatra, had shifted to remote learning, while around 12,800 schools were closed across Sumatra and Borneo. Over 1.4 million students were learning online across affected areas of Indonesia. Since 11 September, haze has reduced visibility in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, to below 1km, disrupting flights for several days and hampering firefighting operations. Although high-confidence fire hotspots declined significantly in Central and West Kalimantan by 14 September, and none were recorded in Riau, fires continued in parts of Kalimantan. Smoke transported from other provinces has also sustained haze in affected areas. Continued fires and cross-provincial smoke are likely to prolong exposure to hazardous air pollution, disrupt transport and education, and constrain firefighting efforts.

vulnerability: Communities near peatlands, plantations, and remote rural settlements in West and Central Kalimantan and Sumatra face repeated seasonal exposure to smoke. Indigenous and forest-dependent groups, including Dayak communities in Kalimantan and Orang Rimba communities in Jambi and South Sumatra, face additional risks because fire can damage the forests and rivers that support their food, water, medicine, and livelihoods. Their distance from health facilities and limited transport and communication links may also delay treatment and restrict access to masks, health information, and clean-air facilities. Prolonged haze and fire damage could further disrupt schooling, transport, farming, fishing, and plantation work, reducing incomes and access to essential services.

Indonesia has comparatively strong response capacity, including national hotspot monitoring, ground and aerial firefighting, cloud seeding, peatland rewetting, health messaging, and law enforcement. Around 48,000 officers, more than 1,400 volunteers, and 34 aircraft had been mobilised by late August. That said, capacity remains uneven at the local level. Remote terrain, limited water, poor visibility, and underground peat fires can delay suppression. Simultaneous outbreaks across several provinces could stretch personnel and aircraft, while fire control operations may not fully address health, education, and livelihood needs..
expected_impact: If the risk materialises, prolonged hazardous haze would primarily affect health, education, transport, and livelihoods across fire-prone areas of Kalimantan and Sumatra.

Repeated exposure to PM2.5 and other pollutants could increase acute respiratory infections, asthma attacks, eye and skin irritation, and cardiovascular complications. Children, older people, pregnant women, outdoor workers, and people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions would face the greatest risk. Persistent hazardous air quality could increase outpatient consultations and hospital admissions and place additional pressure on provincial health services, particularly in remote areas where healthcare access is already limited.

Additional school closures or restrictions on outdoor activity could interrupt learning for children in affected provinces. Dense smoke and reduced visibility could delay or cancel flights, disrupt road and river transport, and constrain access to health facilities, markets, and remote communities. Fire damage and prolonged haze could also reduce household income by interrupting farming, fishing, construction, transport, and plantation work. Localised crop, livestock, or household food stock losses are possible near active fires, but a national or regional food supply crisis is not currently expected.

Indonesia is likely to retain overall leadership of the response. Humanitarian organisations may be required to support respiratory disease surveillance and treatment, the distribution of effective masks, clean-air assistance, risk communication, education continuity, and targeted support to remote, low-income, and Indigenous communities if hazardous conditions persist or local capacity is overwhelmed..

R1072.title: Sustained military pressure in Cabo Delgado drives Islamic State Mozambique attacks on less-exposed communities in Niassa and northern Nampula, causing localised displacement, abductions, and livelihood loss

triggers.title: Increased FADM pressure in northern Cabo Delgado
triggers.description: Continued military operations in Macomia, Muidumbe and surrounding areas could further fragment ISM groups and push fighters towards Quissanga, Meluco, Ancuabe, Chiúre, Montepuez and Niassa. ACLED has documented ISM groups moving south and west following increased state-force pressure in the Catupa area, while subsequent FADM operations also pushed fighters towards Montepuez and the Niassa border. triggers.description: The hunting season in Niassa runs through November, bringing increased activity by hunting camps, tourism operators and associated personnel in remote areas of the Niassa Reserve. This creates a seasonal concentration of people, vehicles and other high-value assets in areas with limited security coverage. The 3 September ISM attack on a hunting camp in Marrupa occurred during the current hunting season, indicating that this seasonal activity can create opportunities for NSAG operations in Niassa. triggers.title: Changes in the coverage of Rwandan and other external security forces
triggers.description: A significant reduction, redeployment or change in operational coverage by Rwandan or other external security forces in Cabo Delgado could create additional space for ISM activity and facilitate movement into southern Cabo Delgado and neighbouring provinces. Rwanda was still rotating personnel into Cabo Delgado in July 2026, while Mozambique has continued to describe the Rwandan deployment as an important component of counter-insurgency operations. Sources: ([taarifa.RW 30/07/2026](https://taarifa.rw/2026/07/30/rwanda-sends-new-contingent-to-mozambique-peacekeeping-mission/), [DW 16/04/2026](https://www.dw.com/en/rwanda-ties-mozambique-troop-deployment-to-eu-funding/a-76795743), [Reuters 19/05/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/rwanda-says-mozambique-has-secured-funds-it-continue-cabo-delgado-mission-2026-05-19/)) Completion rate: 20% Completion rate history: 02-10-2026: 20% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 02-10-2026 Last update: 02-10-2026

rationale: Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) activity in northern Mozambique has increasingly shifted towards mobile, small-group operations as a response to intensified military pressure from Mozambican security forces and their regional partners. Increased patrols, aerial surveillance, and continued counterinsurgency operations have reduced non-state armed groups' capacity to hold territory. As a result, ISM have increasingly dispersed from areas under intensified military pressure in Macomia district towards southern and western Cabo Delgado province. ISM have moved through Quissanga, Mecufi, and Meluco towards Ancuabe and Chiure districts, while other groups moved west towards Montepuez district and subsequently towards Niassa province. One group also crossed into Erati district in Nampula province.

Over the next six months, continued military pressure in Cabo Delgado is expected to further disperse ISM fighters towards areas with weaker security coverage. Remote forested areas and limited state presence in parts of Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, which have had some pockets of attacks, provide opportunities for small groups to move and conduct more attacks. ISM have increasingly targeted informal gold mining sites for looting and ransom, while attacks on vehicles and road users have generated additional income through extortion. In Niassa, the July–November hunting season also increases the presence of hunting camps, tourism operators, and vehicles in remote areas, creating potential high-value targets for ransom and material gains. If ISM establish a presence in Montepuez, Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, these activities could provide alternative sources of revenue and sustain their operations.
vulnerability: Northern Mozambique's capacity to absorb new conflict shocks remains constrained by recurrent displacement, limited access to basic services, and restricted humanitarian access. The 2026 humanitarian response plan targets 1.1 million people across 17 districts in Cabo Delgado, two in Nampula, and one in Niassa by the end of July.

Niassa has comparatively lower conflict exposure than Cabo Delgado but has limited security coverage across its vast rural and conservation areas. The September incursion demonstrated the challenge: troops from the Armed Defence Forces of Mozambique deployed along the Lugenda River were unable to prevent an ISM group from entering Niassa and reaching Marrupa.

Expansion through remote rural and forest areas. ISM's ability to move in small groups through poorly secured areas increases the possibility of attacks beyond the established conflict epicentre. The movement of approximately 30 fighters from Lusaka in Montepuez into Marrupa illustrates this pattern.

Repeated cyclone impacts, including Kenneth (2019), Gombe (2022), and Chido (2024), have damaged homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods across Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Niassa, weakening household coping capacities and recovery efforts. This reduces communities' ability to absorb further displacement and livelihood disruptions resulting from insurgent movements.
expected_impact: Protection risks are likely to increase through killings, abductions, family separation, property destruction, and restrictions on movement, while further operations by the Armed Defence Forces of Mozambique in newly affected areas could expose civilians to clashes, displacement, and disruption of access to livelihoods and services. The September attack in Marrupa already killed two people, abducted 11, and displaced about 2,700 people. Children face an additional risk of abduction and forced recruitment. Recent recruitment and use of children by non-state armed groups has been documented in northern Mozambique, including the abduction of three children in Cabo Delgado in February 2026.

Livelihoods are likely to deteriorate and food insecurity to increase as violence restricts access to farmland, markets, and labour opportunities. In 2025, Marrupa district, Niassa province, had an estimated 110,000 inhabitants, with smallholder agriculture an important source of food and income. Some households in the district were found to depend entirely on small-scale farming after previous climate shocks. Niassa had about 196,000 people in Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3+) between October 2025 and March 2026, equivalent to 12% of its analysed population. Further violence, particularly ahead of the November lean season, could reduce household food stocks, interrupt agricultural activity, and increase market dependence. Disruption is particularly important during the July–November hunting season, which represents a critical seasonal driver of formal revenue and local livelihoods. A persistent ISM presence in Niassa may destabilise the local economy, forcing community displacement and restricting access to vital tourism-dependent livelihoods.

Health services could deteriorate if attacks damage facilities or insecurity prevents health workers and communities from reaching them. The Marrupa attack destroyed a health centre, demonstrating that health infrastructure can be directly affected by ISM attacks; this would remove already limited local capacity rather than necessarily indicating deliberate targeting of health services. In 2025, Niassa had 221 health facilities in total. Of these, four were higher-level referral hospitals: three secondary (district/rural/general) and one tertiary (provincial) hospital, while many communities in Mozambique already travel long distances to reach care. Further displacement and road insecurity could therefore interrupt routine, maternal, and child healthcare, as well as vaccination and emergency referrals.

R1073.title: Accelerated implementation of the E1 settlement plan results in demolitions, displacement of Bedouin communities, and access constraints

triggers.title: Implementation of E1 tender awards before the elections
triggers.description: Progress of the E1 tenders, including any reversal of the Attorney General's postponement, before or after 27 October, could move the plan from approval towards physical implementation and make it more difficult for a future government to reverse. Sources: Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 02-10-2026 Last update: 02-10-2026

triggers.title: Post-election government commitment
triggers.description: If the current government retains power and continues to support E1, it could accelerate planning approvals, infrastructure works, and construction. Sources: Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 02-10-2026 Last update: 02-10-2026

rationale: The E1 settlement plan is a longstanding Israeli initiative that was revived in July 2025 after four years of suspension and approved for advancement by the Israeli Government on 20 August 2025. The plan aims to expand Ma’ale Adumim municipality and create a continuous built-up area between the Israeli settlements and Jerusalem city. Its implementation could further fragment the West Bank, particularly by disrupting geographic contiguity between central and southern areas, and increase the likelihood of severing East Jerusalem from the rest of the occupied West Bank. Its advancement could accelerate the displacement of entire Bedouin communities in the area, generating additional humanitarian needs.

Implementation has accelerated in 2026. In August, Israel issued a tender for 1,234 housing units in E1, followed on 17 September by a further 2,167 units, bringing the total to 3,401. Bidding on the 2,167-unit tender was scheduled to open on 25 October, two days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections.

Government efforts to advance the tenders before the election could accelerate implementation of the approved plan and trigger a faster-paced displacement. The awarding of tenders would allow the Israeli Government to move faster towards infrastructure works and construction, making the project more difficult for a future government to reverse. Implementation could accelerate if the tender process proceeds despite the postponement and the current Government retains power after the election. Court challenges or an election outcome that produces a government less supportive of E1 could, however, delay further implementation.
vulnerability: The West Bank has high and worsening humanitarian needs, with 1.52 million people projected to need humanitarian assistance in 2026, compared with 1.2 million in 2025. Prolonged conflict, displacement, settler violence, settlement expansion, and movement restrictions have significantly eroded household coping capacity.

By September 2026, more than 1,600 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties or property damage had been recorded across the West Bank, affecting 275 Palestinian communities, nearly as many communities as during all of 2025 (279), while more than 4,000 Palestinians had been displaced since the start of the year by demolitions, evictions, settler attacks, and related access restrictions.

E1-affected communities face particularly limited coping capacity. The 18 Bedouin and herding communities living in the area of the planned E1 settlement, comprising about 4,000 people, have experienced sustained demolition and displacement pressure. Between 8–17 September, Israeli authorities demolished 32 structures in South ‘Anata and Tublas villages, displacing 66 Palestinians; both communities are near the area designated for E1 expansion. Access to land, water, and livelihoods is also constrained, mostly because of settler attacks. For example, in July 2026, settler activity damaged water infrastructure serving approximately 200 residents in Nkheila Bedouin community and restricted Palestinian access to grazing areas.

Bedouin communities in the E1/Ma’ale Adumim area rely heavily on grazing and livestock, while restrictions on land and grazing access directly undermine household livelihoods. A 2024 survey of 23 Bedouin communities across the West Bank found that 72% of respondents raise livestock and 59% had been attacked by settlers while grazing. No figure is available for the E1 communities alone..
expected_impact: Implementation of E1 is likely to increase displacement among the approximately 4,000 Palestinians living in 18 Bedouin and herding communities in and around the designated area, through demolitions, evictions, and loss of access to land. Displacement is already being reported near the designated area, with 66 people displaced in South ‘Anata and Tublas between 8–17 September. E1 implementation could increase the frequency and geographic scope of such incidents as construction and associated infrastructure works progress.

Construction of settlements, roads, and related infrastructure could restrict movement between Palestinian communities and reduce access to East Jerusalem, markets, health services, and other essential services such as education. In the first half of 2026, 224 education-related incidents affected 152 schools and 20,450 students across the West Bank, of which 122 involved access restrictions, illustrating the extent to which movement restrictions already disrupt essential services. E1 implementation could create additional checkpoints, road closures, or rerouting around construction areas and settlement infrastructure.

E1 implementation could reduce access to grazing land, agricultural areas, and water resources, undermining the livestock-based livelihoods of affected Bedouin communities and increasing dependence on humanitarian assistance. On 19 July, settlers damaged water pipelines serving approximately 200 residents of Nkheila Bedouin community, restricted access to grazing areas, and took over the nearby Ein Rawabi spring, a key livestock water source. Further loss or fragmentation of grazing areas could reduce livestock holdings and household income and accelerate livelihood displacement.

Protection risks are likely to increase through greater exposure to settler violence, harassment, demolitions, and movement restrictions as settlement construction expands. More than 1,600 settler attacks affecting 275 Palestinian communities were recorded between January and September 2026. In E1-affected communities, implementation could increase encounters between settlers, Palestinians, and security forces, while demolitions and restrictions on access to land and services could expose Palestinians to forced displacement, family separation, and psychosocial distress..

R1074.title: Post-mutiny divisions in Niger's army enable JNIM and ISSP expansion across Tillabéri, Tahoua, and Dosso, driving displacement and restricting humanitarian access

triggers.title: Further military dissent, purges, or command disruption:
triggers.description: Further mutinies, arrests, dismissals, or changes within the Nigerien armed forces could deepen internal divisions and disrupt command continuity and operational coordination. The replacement of armed forces chief of staff Moussa Salaou Barmou and other senior command changes following the August mutiny indicate ongoing restructuring, although their effect on military effectiveness remains unclear. Further changes affecting commanders or units deployed in conflict-affected western regions would increase the likelihood of reduced counterinsurgency capacity. Sources: Completion rate: Completion rate history: Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes. the number of major routes connecting Niamey with Tillabéri, Téra, Ouallam, Banibangou, or Dosso affected by sustained JNIM or ISSP blockades or disruptions. The threshold is at least one strategic route experiencing sustained disruption that significantly restricts civilian movement, military resupply, or humanitarian access. Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 05-10-2026 Last update: 07-10-2026

rationale: The 28–29 August mutiny in Niamey exposed growing divisions within Niger's armed forces that are directly connected to the counterinsurgency front line. Officers and units involved were based in Ouallam and Tera in Tillabéri region and in Dosso region, while grievances included mounting casualties in fighting the Support Group for Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP), as well as perceived preferential treatment of the better-equipped Presidential Guard. Subsequent arrests of soldiers from special forces units in Tillabéri and changes in senior military leadership indicate that the mutiny is already affecting forces deployed in conflict-affected western regions. These divisions are emerging as non-state armed groups intensify pressure across western Niger. Violence remains concentrated in Tillabéri and northern Tahoua, while increasing attacks in Dosso indicate southward expansion. Additional deployments around Niamey, further arrests or command changes, and greater reliance on forces for regime protection could reduce military presence or operational capacity in conflict hotspots, creating additional space for armed groups. Over the next 3–6 months, JNIM and ISSP could exploit reduced or disrupted security force capacity to intensify attacks in existing hotspots in Tillabéri and northern Tahoua and expand their operating space further into Dosso. Increased violence and military operations would generate additional displacement, disrupt livelihoods and access to basic services, and further constrain humanitarian access.
vulnerability: Conflict-affected populations in western Niger already face high humanitarian needs and weakened coping capacity. The 2026 Joint Intersectoral Analysis Framework identifies more than 1.2 million people in need in Tillabéri, including about 226,200 in Tera and 150,100 in Ouallam, two departments directly affected by the current security dynamics. Dosso has nearly 342,000 people in need, while needs are also significant in conflict-affected parts of Tahoua. Insecurity has repeatedly displaced communities, restricted access to farmland and grazing areas, disrupted markets and trade routes, and reduced livelihood opportunities. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity is expected to persist through January 2027 in Tillabéri and northwestern Tahoua, with some displaced households already facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes. Insecurity has contributed to successive agricultural production losses, market disruption, and lower labour income, with poor households reducing meal sizes and expenditure on agriculture, livestock, and health. Humanitarian response capacity to absorb further deterioration is limited. The operating environment became more constrained and the gap between humanitarian needs and available resources widened during the second quarter of 2026. Insecurity continues to restrict access to affected communities, while displacement is increasing pressure on host communities. Dosso remains comparatively more resilient than Tillabéri and northwestern Tahoua, but the southward expansion of violence could increasingly disrupt livelihoods and markets there.
expected_impact: Displacement is expected to increase in Tillabéri, northwestern Tahoua, and areas of Dosso affected by expanding insecurity. More than 85,000 people were displaced in Tillabéri alone between October 2025 and early 2026, illustrating the scale of population movements that recent insecurity can generate. If insecurity intensifies over the next 3–6 months, displacement would remain predominantly local, towards departmental centres and safer host communities, including Tera and its outskirts, Tahoua town and Tchintabaraden, and Dogondoutchi from affected areas of Dosso. Populations remaining in areas where ISSP consolidates or expands its influence would face heightened protection risks associated with coercive control. In Tillabéri and northern Tahoua, this could include increased taxation and livestock seizures, ultimatums to leave villages, restrictions on movement and access to livelihoods, alongside direct attacks against civilians. These practices could further erode household assets and contribute to additional displacement. Insecurity during the October–January harvest and post-harvest period could deepen food insecurity in Tillabéri and northwestern Tahoua, where IPC 3 outcomes are already expected through January 2027 and some displaced households face IPC 4. Reduced access to fields could leave crops unharvested, accelerate household stock depletion, and increase earlier-than-usual market dependence, potentially resulting in an earlier or deeper lean season. In Dosso, expanding insecurity could disrupt agricultural production and cross-border trade, particularly around Dioundiou and Gaya and along routes connecting Niger with Benin and Nigeria. Reduced trade flows could constrain market supply and increase transport costs, including for markets supplying Dosso and Niamey. Humanitarian access could deteriorate along routes serving Tera, Ouallam, Tillabéri, and Banibangou, and along the Niamey–Dosso road, disrupting humanitarian deliveries and reducing the regularity and geographical coverage of assistance.

replies.text: Fair point on fuel, but repeated strikes near the border don't fit a simple supply dispute.

comments.name: Patient Kestrel
comments.text: I agreed at first, but the point about supply routes here changed my mind. Most of what I hear around Tine is about fuel and smuggling disputes, not fighters trying to hold ground inside Chad. Worrying, but not sustained confrontation yet.

comments.name: Hidden Falcon
comments.text: I've seen this pattern on other borders. Once armed groups depend on a crossing for supplies, it stops being a border incident and becomes a target. The infrastructure trigger is the one I'd watch: a strike on Amdjarass would change the whole picture.

replies.name: Hidden Stork
replies.text: Amdjarass is the one I'd watch too. A strike there would hit aid flights as well as the headlines.

comments.name: Wise Kestrel
comments.text: Agree, and the economic side deserves more weight. When a conflict runs on fuel and gold routes, the fighting follows the money. If those corridors close, prices in the border towns will move long before the headlines do.

comments.name: Southern Gazelle
comments.text: Agree. Working in Niger, I've seen how quickly a border area changes once armed groups move freely, and how slowly humanitarian access comes back afterwards. I'd plan for access problems before casualties rise.

replies.name: Patient Stork
replies.text: Same pattern elsewhere in the Sahel. Access took far longer to come back than the fighting took to move on.

comments.name: Clear Falcon
comments.text: Attached a situation update. Families in West Darfur are deciding on rumours as much as on attacks, so one strike near Adré could move people in both directions at once. Refugees and returnees would need help on the same road.

replies.name: Southern Gazelle
replies.text: We hear the same on the Chad side. Rumours about registration can move people as fast as shelling does.

comments.name: Calm Stork
comments.text: Attached a market bulletin that fits this reading. Supply routes are where armed groups earn and spend, so markets often show trouble early. I know this pattern from Colombia's border regions more than from Chad, so take it as a comparison.

comments.name: Keen Oryx
comments.text: Agree with the rating, but I'd add local deals to the picture. In Syria, crossings changed hands through negotiation as often as through fighting, and civilians were caught out either way. Could the same happen around Tine?

comments.name: Amber Jackal
comments.text: The rains are over, so the tracks around Adré are passable again. That helps aid trucks, but it helps armed groups too. Sites in Ouaddaï and Wadi Fira are already overcrowded, so new arrivals would have nowhere to go.

replies.name: Sharp Otter
replies.text: Worth checking with partners in Adré first. Some tracks may still be cut after the last storms.
